- preferred clarification style.

Keep private overlays separate from the shared catalog, attach TTL/freshness, provide inspection/deletion, and never let a pattern imply authorization or override an explicit current request.

## 5M and 40M corpus architecture

The scale target changes the physical design. Do not treat 40 million primitives as a larger SQLite demo, and do not store many full-precision vectors for every artifact without a tiering plan.

### Order of physical narrowing

``` text
physical scope / authorization partition
  -> lifecycle and risk bitmap
  -> exact ID / digest / history maps
  -> type, effect, environment, language, domain partitions
  -> lexical / sparse postings and LSH buckets
  -> coarse semantic shard or centroid
  -> ANN inside eligible shards
  -> exact or stronger rerank of a small shortlist
  -> graph expansion and route compile
```

Apply isolation-critical predicates physically or before result disclosure. Approximate filtering after ANN can reduce recall and can leak workload-dependent behavior across tenants. Recheck authorization after fusion and before materialization as defense in depth.

### Memory reality

Approximate raw vector payload, before ANN graph, IDs, metadata, alignment, replication, or allocator overhead:

| Corpus | One 384-d float32 view | One 768-d float32 view | Five 768-d float32 views |
|-------:|-----------------------:|-----------------------:|-------------------------:|
|     5M |                7.68 GB |               15.36 GB |                  76.8 GB |
|    40M |               61.44 GB |              122.88 GB |                 614.4 GB |

This does not rule out multi-view retrieval. It means Taedri should tier it:

- store exact, type, bitmap, lexical, sparse, and LSH structures for the whole catalog;
- keep one compact/quantized routing vector broadly;
- retain richer facet vectors for hot, curated, high-value, or ambiguous regions;
- use float16, scalar/product quantization, OPQ, or binary/coarse codes where held-out recall permits;
- use HNSW for hot/smaller shards when its memory/latency curve wins;
- benchmark IVF-PQ/OPQ, disk ANN, and partitioned indexes for the cold 40M tier;
- rerank the shortlist with original vectors or a stronger model; and
- start late-interaction storage only on curated regions or an on-demand cache.

At 5M and 40M, measure recall against exact search on representative subsets while sweeping vector dimension, precision, quantization, HNSW `M`/`efSearch`, IVF list/probe counts, shard count, filter selectivity, and update churn. No production path should require a full scan.

### Recommended stores

| Need                              | Data structure                               | Notes                                           |
|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| ID/digest/name/version            | Hash/B-tree maps                             | Exact and negative caches; deterministic        |
| Tenant/lifecycle/effect/risk/type | Partition keys + Roaring-style bitmaps       | Hard intersection before ranking                |
| Text and sparse semantics         | Inverted index with WAND/early termination   | Separate fields and analyzers                   |
| Typos/substrings                  | Character n-gram/trigram index               | Preserve a technical-token view                 |
| Near duplicates/set overlap       | MinHash/weighted MinHash/SimHash buckets     | Recompute exact similarity after block          |
| Coarse semantics                  | Centroid/taxonomy/quantized routing codes    | Select candidate shards                         |
| Dense semantics                   | HNSW or IVF-PQ/disk ANN by tier              | Benchmark, do not universalize                  |
| Contracts/routes                  | Typed graph + adjacency/reachability indexes | Expand necessary connectors                     |
| History                           | Scoped relational/event store                | Store successes, failures, expiry, modification |
| Receipts                          | Append-only, content-addressed records       | Replay, audit, counterfactual evaluation        |

### Partition strategy

Candidate partitions may use:

- tenant or authorization domain;
- artifact kind and lifecycle;
- task domain and language;
- programming language/runtime/platform;
- input and output type families;
- effect and risk classes;
- standard/framework/package family; and
- hot/warm/cold usage tier.

Partitions must have multi-partition fallback. A coarse classifier that chooses one wrong shard should not destroy recall. Retrieve the top few plausible partitions and retain an OOD path.

### Caches and invalidation

Cache:

- canonical `QueryPlan` by request digest;
- task-family and clause extraction;
- local query embeddings and sparse vectors;
- per-view candidate lists;
- fused body-free candidate sets;
- compatible route graphs;
- compiled recipes;
- negative results; and
- final validated results where semantics permit.

Every cache key must include the relevant tenant/policy, catalog/index epoch, artifact closure, environment, lifecycle, and oracle/evidence versions. A stale cheap answer is more expensive than a fresh fallback.

## Token reduction beyond query writing

The complete token strategy has five levers.

### A. Eliminate model calls

- exact result replay;
- exact compiled-recipe replay;
- deterministic QueryPlan compilation;
- exact IDs and typed templates;
- body-free graph compilation;
- deterministic execution and oracle;
- negative cache/no-match decisions; and
- compile a missing reusable unit once rather than regenerate per use.

### B. Shrink model input when a call remains

- send an `AmbiguityCertificate`, not the entire search transcript;
- use body-free cards and short request-bound handles;
- include only fields that distinguish the remaining candidates;
- send plan deltas rather than the full accumulated state;
- reuse a stable cached prefix where the provider supports it;
- cap candidate count by byte budget as well as item count;
- summarize retrieval disagreement deterministically;
- omit already resolved constraints;
- bind artifacts by digest rather than pasting bodies; and
- segment long prompts so only relevant clauses reach the fallback.

### C. Shrink model output

- return enum values, spans, handles, or AST patches;
- one call emits all bounded query variants;
- grammar-bound maximum of two to four variants;
- no prose rationale unless it improves verification;
- deterministic compiler and route solver perform integration; and
- request the smallest distinguishing clarification instead of a full plan.

### D. Amortize intelligence

- compile aliases, embeddings, expansions, and type graphs offline;
- cache successful query deltas as reviewed templates;
- distill repeated fallbacks into local classifiers or dictionaries;
- persist successful recipes and negative results;
- reuse session-level QueryPlans and clause embeddings; and
- separate one-time foundry cost from per-use execution.

### E. Reduce fallback probability

- multi-view lexical/code/semantic indexing;
- top-k per capability and graph-safe connector expansion;
- guarded history and prototype retrieval;
- calibrated hybrid fusion;
- local targeted reranking;
- tool-derived exact facts; and
- one high-information clarification.

The input side is often the bigger production lever. In prior Taedri session experiments, compact capability cards reduced repeated input volume far more than signatures-only source exposure and without asking a model to reimplement missing behavior. Preserve that principle here: the selector sees proof-bearing distinctions, not implementation text.

## `RetrievalTierReceipt`

Every tier should emit a composable receipt:

``` json
{
  "schema_version": "taedri.retrieval-tier-receipt/v1",
  "request_digest": "sha256:...",
  "query_plan_digest": "sha256:...",
  "tier_id": "C2.dense-ann.capability",
  "tier_version": "...",
  "catalog_epoch": "...",
  "policy_digest": "sha256:...",

    "cpu_ms": 3.1,
    "gpu_ms": 8.7,
```

Keep provider and local model tokens separate. Retain raw scores, ranks, calibrator versions, and contribution provenance in an attached detail record. Receipts enable exact cascade accounting, debugging, counterfactual policy evaluation, and regression tests.

## Experiments that can prove the waterfall

### Benchmark arms

Freeze these cumulative and diagnostic arms:

1.  `always_large_query_writer`: current model-first query planning and selection comparator.
2.  `exact_replay_only`: exact result/recipe/ID/history with full revalidation.
3.  `structured_templates`: deterministic extraction, hard filters, types, and templates.
4.  `classic_local`: plus BM25/FTS, keyphrases, code, morphology, fuzzy, and LSH.
5.  `learned_sparse`: plus SPLADE-style retrieval.
6.  `dense_ann`: plus multi-view local dense retrieval.
7.  `hybrid_rrf`: sparse+dense+classic producer-grouped RRF.
8.  `graph_history`: plus typed graph expansion and scoped recipe priors.
9.  `guarded_feedback`: one PRF/ontology expansion pass when coherent.
10. `local_rerank`: late interaction or cross-encoder on a bounded shortlist.
11. `local_slot_filler`: grammar-bound unresolved-slot patch.
12. `hosted_query_delta`: one bounded final query-expansion call.
13. `compile_once_then_execute`: new reusable implementation, then repeated execution.
14. `bypass`: direct/from-scratch result when reuse is uneconomic.

Add two focused composition suites:

**Black-box sufficiency:** compare description only; signature only; description+signature; verified public contract; contract+one example; contract+selected failure/effect evidence; and full source. Vary route length/topology and measure compile acceptance, oracle pass, unsafe route, and tokens.

**Route presentation:** freeze the same valid routes and compare route IDs; compact summaries; contrastive route deltas; primitive cards; chosen route nodes+validated adjacency; and the full validated subgraph. This isolates prompt representation from retrieval/solver quality.

Run the same requests through every frozen arm. Store later-tier outputs even when an earlier tier would have stopped, so stopping policies can be evaluated counterfactually offline.

### Required task strata

Include real and adversarial cases with:

- exact IDs, digests, standards, quoted strings, and known recipes;
- lexical overlap and vocabulary mismatch;
- paraphrases and long compound prompts;
- typos, punctuation/case differences, abbreviations, and multilingual text;
- code, imports, stack traces, paths, CLI flags, schema fields, and error codes;
- explicit negation, exclusions, versions, units, and effect boundaries;
- multi-hop typed routes and low-ranked necessary connectors;
- multiple valid routes and one subtly invalid near match;
- stale policy, environment, dependency, artifact, and oracle cases;
- cross-tenant decoys and unauthorized high-similarity candidates;
- at least 20–30% true no-match/missing-implementation cases;
- OOD task families; and
- adversarial query expansion/topic-drift cases.

### Primary metrics

Retrieval and routing:

- eligible component recall@5/20/100;
- `eligible_route_recall@k` and at fixed candidate-byte budgets;
- precision@5/20 and MRR;
- unique-route rate;
- exact replay and no-match rates;
- final local-model and hosted-model reach rates;
- false reuse per request and per automatic decision;
- abstention coverage, selective risk, and risk-coverage curve;
- calibration log loss, Brier score, reliability plots, and ECE;
- route stability under benign query perturbations; and
- oracle pass, forbidden-effect, rollback, and user-modification rates.

Cost and system behavior:

- provider input/output/reasoning/cached tokens and dollars;
- local model tokens, CPU/GPU time, utilization, estimated dollars, and energy;
- query-plan, card, recipe, and body bytes;
- implementation bytes exposed to any model;
- p50/p95/p99 cold and warm latency;
- index bytes, build time, update lag, tombstone behavior, and stale-hit rate;
- failures, repairs, fallbacks, and recovery cost; and
- incremental eligible-route recall per millisecond, dollar, provider token, and index byte.

Report overall metrics and every task/risk/language slice. Averages can conceal exactly the rare hard requests that reach expensive or dangerous tiers.

### Scale tests

Run at 1M, 5M, 10M, 40M, and optionally 100M stress scale with:

- cold and warm caches;
- tenant partitions and skew;
- concurrent reads and catalog churn;
- inserts, revocations, replacements, and tombstones;
- index/receipt lag;
- ANN filter selectivity; and
- exact-search recall checks on stratified subsets.

At 40M, the production acceptance gate is no full scan, stable tail latency, zero unauthorized disclosure, and non-inferior eligible-route recall under churn.

### Statistical protocol

1.  Freeze request set, catalog, index, policies, providers/models, prices, prompts, and artifacts.
2.  Split temporally and by demand family to prevent history and paraphrase leakage.
3.  Train fusion/EVSI models only on out-of-fold predictions.
4.  Select thresholds on tuning/calibration data, then lock them before final test.
5.  Use independent deterministic or hidden-fixture oracles where possible and blinded adjudication otherwise.
6.  Pair every arm on the same task instances and report bootstrap confidence intervals clustered by family.
7.  Require quality non-inferiority and a false-reuse upper bound before claiming savings.
8.  Include failed compilation, invalidation, repair, verification, and recovery in the numerator.
9.  For live provider claims, use exact provider token receipts; do not estimate from characters.
10. Plot cumulative tokens, dollars, latency, failures, and oracle passes at reuse counts 1, 5, 10, 17, 100, and 1,000.

The complete configuration space is approximately:

``` text
context policy
  x demand parser
  x shortcut policy
  x retrieval action set/order
  x fusion/calibration
  x hard-filter policy
  x graph representation/planner
  x candidate and edge budgets
  x disclosure policy
  x selector/model tier
  x execution/verification policy
  x cache state
  x history/personalization policy
```

Do not run its full Cartesian product. Use unit ablations, frozen-candidate presentation tests, frozen-presentation retrieval tests, pairwise/covering-array interaction designs, successive halving to remove dominated configurations, and Bayesian optimization only over remaining safe continuous weights/thresholds. Finish with champion/challenger shadow and paired live tests.

### Marginal-value table to publish

For each added tier, show:

| Tier | Reached % | Correctly resolved % of reached | False accept % | Eligible route recall delta | Hosted calls avoided | Provider tokens avoided | Local cost added | p95 latency delta | Decision |
|------|----------:|--------------------------------:|---------------:|----------------------------:|---------------------:|------------------------:|-----------------:|------------------:|----------|

This table will reveal layers that sound sophisticated but do not earn their cost.

## Concrete build plan

### First vertical slice

Before building every tier, prove one end-to-end task family with:

1.  `ContextManifestV1`, `DemandIRV1`, and derived `QueryPlanV1`;
2.  50–500 logical primitives represented by verified `PrimitiveCardV1` records and port-level edges;
3.  exact/history plus fielded FTS/BM25 and typed bidirectional graph search;
4.  `GraphIRV1` supporting a linear route plus one branch/join and one retry/fallback case;
5.  exact replay, deterministic route solve, and gap-directed retrieval;
6.  route-handle disclosure at 1/2/4/8 alternatives and L0/L1/L2 detail;
7.  three selector actions: deterministic, local constrained SLM, and one strong hosted model;
8.  post-selection body resolution, sandbox execution, and independent oracle; and
9.  exact cost/token/disclosure/stop/failure receipts.

This slice answers the central questions before 40M-scale infrastructure: can compact contracts support correct composition, what candidate/detail budget works, and how often is any model actually needed?

### Wave 0 — fix the decision boundary (1–3 days)

- Preserve the existing max-normalized combiner only as a named diagnostic baseline.
- Forbid its score from authorizing execution or satisfying a confidence threshold.
- Separate eligibility filters, candidate retrieval, route feasibility, route ranking, and stopping in the API.
- Add `good_accept`, `false_accept`, `continue`, provider/local cost, latency, and stop reason to receipts.
- Keep exact ID, mandatory contracts, authorization, lifecycle, and effects as gates.
- Add regression tests where a weak top signal becomes `1.0` and where an irrelevant outlier flips A/B under max normalization.

### Wave 1 — compile requests, do not draft queries (3–7 days)

- Implement `ContextManifestV1` and canonical `DemandIRV1`; derive `QueryPlanV1` rather than treating it as the entire demand.
- Implement `QueryPlanV1`, provenance-bearing spans, unresolved slots, and budgets.
- Implement raw/NFC/search/code-preserving normalization views.
- Add ID, digest, package, symbol, error, type, I/O, negation, version, standard, effect, and environment extractors.
- Build a parameterized QueryPlan-to-query-AST compiler.
- Add request, recipe, exact-ID, historical, and negative-result caches with versioned keys.
- Add `AmbiguityCertificateV1`.
- Define `PrimitiveCardV1`, `PrimitiveEdgeV1`, logical-identity/variant rules, and a minimal port-level hypergraph schema.
- Define `GraphIRV1`, route digests, and static schema/type/effect validation for the first route shapes.

Suggested modules:

``` text
taedri_platform/retrieval/query_plan.py
taedri_platform/retrieval/query_compiler.py
taedri_platform/retrieval/extractors.py
taedri_platform/retrieval/ambiguity.py
taedri_platform/retrieval/receipts.py
```

### Wave 2 — strong zero-model retrieval (1–2 weeks)

- Build fielded SQLite FTS5/BM25 for the first proof and a scale-portable backend contract.
- Add exact phrase, proximity, prefix, field, Boolean, and negative-clause templates.
- Add punctuation-aware character n-grams, fuzzy aliases, code symbol/path/import indexes, and keyphrase/entity views.
- Add MinHash/SimHash blocking with exact post-block similarity.
- Implement independent per-signal and per-required-capability quotas.
- Implement producer-grouped weighted RRF with full contribution receipts.
- Expand typed connectors before global truncation.
- Add `eligible_route_recall@budget` to the harness.
- Add exact pack/template replay, forward/backward/bidirectional graph solving, deterministic route dominance, and typed gap-directed search.

### Wave 3 — semantic and historical layers (2–4 weeks)

- Add a frozen local embedding adapter with separate capability, I/O, effect, standard, and error views.
- Benchmark HNSW and IVF-PQ/quantization at the first scale point.
- Add a SPLADE-style learned sparse arm.
- Add the scoped success/failure history store and Beta posterior/freshness logic.
- Add graph neighborhood and reachability indexes.
- Implement guarded PRF as one optional action with drift tests.
- Measure every layer's incremental route recall and fallthrough reduction.

### Wave 4 — calibrated stopping and local ambiguity reduction (3–6 weeks)

- Build out-of-fold per-retriever calibrators.
- Train a transparent route-level stacker before a more complex learning-to-rank model.
- Add route risk-coverage thresholds per family/risk tier.
- Add stability/OOD features and a conservative stop state machine.
- Add a local cross-encoder/late-interaction reranker for top 20–100 body-free cards.
- Add a lightweight next-action/EVSI predictor in shadow mode.
- Add a grammar-bound local slot filler that can patch only unresolved enums and spans.
- Add the active disclosure controller: route counts, L0–L3 detail, differentiating-field acquisition, ordering, and progressive expansion.
- Add a vendor-neutral model registry and broker covering deterministic, discriminative, SLM, cheap hosted, strong, and frontier actions.
- Build frozen-candidate composition and candidate/edge/detail/duplicate benchmarks before enabling learned routing.

### Wave 5 — bounded hosted fallback and distillation (after gates pass)

- Implement one hosted `QueryDelta` call with a strict JSON schema, two-to-four variant cap, no bodies, and a small output budget.
- Deterministically validate, compile, and run its deltas once.
- Treat generated entities/facts as retrieval hypotheses, never truth.
- Cache successful deltas and send them through review/distillation into aliases, prototypes, templates, dictionaries, or local training data.
- Make every expensive fallback file an “eliminate me” candidate with measured frequency and payoff.

### Wave 6 — 5M/40M production hardening

- Build physical authorization and lifecycle partitions plus bitmap filters.
- Add hot/warm/cold semantic storage and compressed ANN.
- Benchmark shard routing with multi-shard/OOD fallback.
- Add churn, revocation, tombstone, and index-lag receipts.
- Run shadow, low-risk canary, then expand by risk tier only when confidence bounds pass.
- Add thin host adapters for `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`, path rules, skills, hooks, MCP meta-tools/resources, and bounded agents; keep the canonical policy and receipts vendor-neutral.
- Add event-sourced invalidation, scoped user/project history overlays, and private cache partitioning.

## Acceptance criteria

Before making the waterfall the default:

- zero unauthorized candidates disclosed at every tier;
- zero implementation bodies exposed before compilation;
- exact replay and deterministic unique-route paths use zero provider tokens;
- eligible-route recall@100 is non-inferior to the run-all retriever oracle within a predeclared margin;
- automatic route false-reuse upper bound meets the per-risk target;
- hosted query drafting rate is measured and materially below model-first;
- provider token/dollar savings lower confidence bound is positive;
- local compute plus latency stays within declared budgets;
- no full scan at production corpus size;
- every stop and escalation is reproducible from receipts; and
- same-task paired hidden-oracle results pass with failures and fallbacks included.

## High-value ideation backlog

1.  **Query prototype library.** Cluster successful `QueryPlan`s and retrieve the nearest validated prototype before interpreting from scratch.
2.  **Differentiating-predicate index.** Precompute the fields that distinguish routes within a compatibility region; produce better ambiguity certificates and one-question clarifications.
3.  **Queryless contract cells.** For common `(start_type, end_type, capabilities, effects, environment)` combinations, precompute eligible candidate regions and route skeletons.
4.  **Capability bitmap/Bloom precheck.** Reject shards that cannot possibly cover all required capabilities before lexical or ANN work. Any Bloom result is only a negative/partition hint; exact verification remains required.
5.  **Semantic memoization by clause.** Hash normalized prompt clauses and reuse facet embeddings independently across requests and sessions.
6.  **Minimal sufficient candidate cards.** Learn which body-free fields affect selection, but retain all proof fields required for validation.
7.  **Consensus certificate.** Record which independent retriever families and exact predicates support every route component, not merely a fused score.
8.  **Counterfactual late-tier logging.** On a sample, run later local tiers even after an early stop to estimate missed value and recalibrate without exposing users to experimental decisions.
9.  **Active-learning queue.** Send high-frequency/high-cost ambiguity clusters to template, ontology, metadata, or primitive-quality work rather than repeatedly paying model fallbacks.
10. **Negative knowledge assets.** Persist verified no-match, incompatibility, revoked, and misleading-alias examples; they are as valuable as positive recipes.
11. **Bounded semantic hashing.** Test binary/quantized codes as a coarse block, then exact-vector rerank. Do not use the hash collision as final semantic evidence.
12. **Cross-family adapter discovery.** When graph compilation repeatedly misses one type conversion, nominate an adapter primitive for foundry creation.
13. **Risk-tiered cascades.** Low-risk suggestion traffic can accept broader calibrated coverage; destructive/external-effect routes require exact contracts, authorization, transaction/sandbox controls, and independent verification regardless of similarity.
14. **Privacy-tiered cascades.** Keep exact, lexical, tools, embeddings, and small models local by default; hosted escalation requires an explicit policy and redacted ambiguity input.
15. **Contextual routing later.** Once complete action/outcome/propensity logging exists, learn which safe next tier to run. Begin with shadow selection among a small set of frozen cascades, not unconstrained online RL.

## What to keep and what to change in the current implementation

### Keep

- body-free card retrieval;
- independent signal provenance;
- typed compatibility and unique-route compilation;
- explicit abstention on equal valid routes;
- exact authorization checks;
- compact handle recipes;
- digest-checked post-compile body resolution;
- zero implementation-body exposure to the selector;
- deterministic execution and independent oracle; and
- semantic and historical paths as pluggable producers.

### Change now

- replace max-normalized weighted sums as the production fusion/stop signal;
- prevent exact IDs and mandatory contracts from behaving like ordinary soft weights;
- add hard prefilters before ranking and rechecks after fusion;
- preserve candidates per signal/capability and expand graph connectors before truncation;
- make history a scoped posterior with failures, recency, and invalidation;
- add negative evidence and signal applicability/abstention;
- calibrate on route success, not candidate similarity;
- add a formal stop/escalate receipt;
- measure semantic and history branches in separate fixtures; and
- run a live paired repeated-use curve before claiming provider savings.

### Current proof status

The attached proof—46 catalog candidates, a unique five-step route, a nine-byte handle recipe, 8,344 implementation bytes loaded only after compilation, zero model calls/tokens/body exposure, and a passing independent oracle—demonstrates the mechanism on one controlled fixture. It does not yet establish corpus-scale recall, fallback rate, risk calibration, or a live provider-dollar percentage. The next proof is the cumulative benchmark above.

## Product statement to target

> Taedri compiles each request into `DemandIR`, a typed retrieval program, and verified GraphIR over opaque implementations with transparent contracts. It searches broadly outside the model, exposes only decision-changing route evidence, and stops only on an authorized, compatible, calibrated route. Routine reuse and deterministic composition consume zero provider tokens; free-form query/planning is reserved for the measured unresolved tail, bounded to a small delta, and distilled into future deterministic assets.

That is both stronger and more defensible than “we use a smaller LLM to write queries.”

# Alternatives to Every Component in the Taedri First Vertical Slice

> **ANNEX STATUS — ALTERNATIVE DESIGN ATLAS.** “Recommended” means a design choice
> for evaluation, not a current feature or launch commitment. Part 0 remains the
> implementation and evidence authority.

**Architecture decision addendum — 2026-07-15**

## Executive answer

The proposed vertical slice is a strong, balanced design, but none of its named components is mandatory and several of the bundles conceal independent decisions. The seven bullets actually contain at least nineteen replaceable choices:

1.  `ContextManifest`
2.  `DemandIR`
3.  verified `PrimitiveCard`
4.  port-level hypergraph
5.  `GraphIR`
6.  exact lookup
7.  historical reuse
8.  fielded BM25
9.  typed bidirectional route solving
10. route handles
11. the fixed `1/2/4/8` candidate schedule
12. multiple detail levels
13. deterministic selector
14. local-SLM selector
15. strong-model selector
16. post-selection body resolution
17. execution
18. independent verification
19. exact receipts

There are three kinds of alternative:

- **Replacement:** another mechanism performs the same job, such as a cross-encoder replacing a local generative SLM for selection.
- **Collapse:** two layers become one, such as a typed request envelope containing both context references and demand constraints.
- **Deletion:** the system proves that a layer is unnecessary, such as exact replay eliminating retrieval, route generation, and selection.

Deletion is usually the largest token saving. The target architecture should therefore be a lattice of fast exits rather than a mandatory procession through all nineteen components.

My preferred first implementation is slightly simpler than the original proposal:

> Use one schema-validated `RequestEnvelope` with a demand projection and acceptance tests; standard interface contracts plus verification evidence; a relational port index that can project a hypergraph only when required; a tiny plan DAG lowered to an existing runtime; exact/pack/history/lexical retrieval followed by typed search; adaptive, diversity-aware route presentation; no-selector and deterministic baselines plus a local non-generative ranker, local SLM, cheap hosted model, and strong fallback; lazy content-addressed body loading; deterministic execution oracles; and operational traces plus cryptographically bound provenance.

That recommendation is not a rejection of `ContextManifest`, `DemandIR`, `PrimitiveCard`, the hypergraph, or `GraphIR`. It is a warning against prematurely turning useful logical concepts into five new, independently persisted platforms.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The quickest decision map

| Original choice                | Delete/collapse option                        | Lightweight replacement                           | Platform/standards replacement                | Formal/heavy replacement                                      | Keep the original when…                                                            |
|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ContextManifest`              | Retrieve context lazily; no up-front manifest | Request envelope with typed references            | CloudEvents/event log; relational snapshot    | RDF/PROV knowledge graph; blackboard with truth maintenance   | Many context sources conflict, expire, or have different authority                 |
| `DemandIR`                     | Direct trigger or task template               | Intent + slots + constraints + acceptance tests   | JSON Schema/Protobuf/Avro record              | PDDL problem, CSP/SMT model, goal graph                       | Cross-domain demand must be model-independent and testable                         |
| Verified `PrimitiveCard`       | Function signature or direct handle           | JSON contract + examples + evidence refs          | OpenAPI/MCP/IDL/Wasm component contract       | Design-by-contract, refinement type, proof-carrying component | Retrieval, composition, policy, and audit need one compact projection              |
| Port-level hypergraph          | No graph; template/pack lookup                | Relational compatibility table or bipartite graph | Property graph/dataflow DAG                   | Petri net, RDF/SHACL, session types, AND/OR graph             | Multi-input joins, alternatives, effects, and resource constraints are first-class |
| `GraphIR`                      | Execute a known pack directly                 | Tiny DAG/recipe JSON or generated code            | CWL/WDL/ASL/BPMN/Temporal/Argo                | PDDL/HTN plan, Petri net, e-graph/MLIR                        | Multiple planners and runtimes require one stable interchange layer                |
| Exact lookup                   | None                                          | Hash map/registry/SQL key                         | Content-addressed registry                    | Certified name resolution                                     | Stable handles and canonical IDs exist                                             |
| History                        | Stateless operation                           | Exact recipe cache                                | Event-sourced route/result store              | Contextual bandit/Bayesian policy/frequent-subgraph learner   | Repeated demand families are common and validity can be rechecked                  |
| Fielded BM25                   | Direct filters or graph lookup                | SQLite FTS5/BM25F                                 | Lucene/OpenSearch                             | Learned sparse retrieval, late interaction                    | Descriptions, types, standards, errors, and names carry strong lexical signals     |
| Typed bidirectional solver     | Pack/template or single-hop lookup            | Forward/backward BFS, Dijkstra, A\*               | Workflow planner or database recursive query  | CP-SAT, SMT, ILP, HTN/PDDL                                    | Routes are multi-step and typed end constraints prune search materially            |
| Route handles                  | Deterministic winner; show nothing            | Route IDs or compact cards                        | Paginated tool/API                            | Proof-carrying plan                                           | A model must choose without seeing implementation bodies                           |
| `1/2/4/8` alternatives         | One winner only                               | Fixed top-k                                       | Token-budget or probability-mass cutoff       | Contextual policy learned per task/model                      | You are running a clean cardinality experiment, not declaring a constant           |
| Multiple detail levels         | One fixed compact view                        | Summary + delta                                   | Interactive progressive disclosure            | Formal proof object                                           | Ambiguity sometimes requires more evidence but bodies must stay hidden             |
| Deterministic selector         | Unique route; no selection                    | Weighted score/Pareto rules                       | Optimizer/policy engine                       | CP-SAT/SMT objective                                          | Constraints and objective can be stated without semantic judgment                  |
| Local-SLM selector             | Non-generative ranker                         | Constrained local classifier/SLM                  | On-device inference service                   | Ensemble/cascade                                              | Some residual semantic comparison remains after retrieval and solving              |
| Strong-model selector          | Clarify or ask user                           | Cheap hosted model                                | Frontier model with tool pagination           | Committee/debate                                              | Remaining ambiguity is valuable enough to justify provider spend                   |
| Post-selection body resolution | Eager load or remote call                     | Lazy digest-bound loader                          | Package manager, OCI, Wasm component          | Capability-secure linker                                      | Bodies are large, privileged, proprietary, or frequently changing                  |
| Execution                      | Return a plan only                            | In-process/subprocess                             | Existing workflow/runtime platform            | Verified interpreter/sandbox                                  | The product must actually perform side effects, not merely recommend               |
| Independent verification       | Trust execution result                        | Schema/assertion/unit oracle                      | Property/fuzz/differential/external validator | Model checking or proof checking                              | A false success is costly and verification can use a different failure mode        |
| Exact receipts                 | Plain logs or aggregate metrics               | Structured event record                           | OpenTelemetry + provider usage + provenance   | Signed/Merkle/in-toto/SLSA attestations                       | Cost, inputs, decisions, artifacts, and effects must be reproducible or auditable  |

# 1. Alternatives to `ContextManifest`

## What job it is doing

`ContextManifest` is not merely “the prompt.” It is a control-plane view of which facts, instructions, preferences, resources, memories, policies, and evidence are applicable to this request. Its distinctive value is selectivity and provenance: context can be referenced without copying all of its text into every model call.

The design mistake to avoid is treating “manifest” as synonymous with “one large JSON document.” The logical function can be implemented many ways.

## Alternative A — no manifest; lazy context retrieval

Start with the current request and resolve context only when a route, primitive, or verifier asks for it.

**Wins:** lowest up-front latency; avoids spending work on irrelevant context; fits tool-using agents that can inspect files or memory on demand.

**Loses:** repeated reads; harder conflict detection; a planner may not know that a decisive constraint exists; reproducibility requires logging every later resolution.

**Use when:** tasks are short, context sources are few, and tools can fetch exact facts cheaply.

## Alternative B — a single typed `RequestEnvelope`

Collapse context and demand into one record:

``` yaml
request_id: req_123
utterance_ref: blob:sha256:...
goal: transform_dataset
inputs: [...]
outputs: [...]
constraints: [...]
acceptance_tests: [...]
context_refs:
  - ref: project-rules:sha256:...
    role: instruction
    authority: project
    freshness: 2026-07-15T12:00:00Z
policy_snapshot_ref: policy:sha256:...
```

This is likely the best first slice. It preserves typed references, scope, and freshness without maintaining two elaborate object models. JSON Schema is specifically designed to describe and validate JSON document structure, constraints, and annotations, so it is a natural baseline for this envelope ([JSON Schema 2020-12 Core](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core)).

## Alternative C — intent/slot frame

Use a compact semantic frame such as:

``` text
intent=publish_report
object=sales_dataset
audience=board
format=pdf
deadline=today
must=[cite_sources, preserve_brand]
must_not=[external_upload]
```

**Wins:** very small, easy to classify locally, excellent for a bounded product surface.

**Loses:** long-tail goals do not fit the ontology; nuanced evidence and contradictory instructions are awkward.

**Use when:** 80–95% of traffic falls into a known set of request families.

## Alternative D — acceptance-test-first demand

Represent the request by examples and pass/fail criteria rather than an exhaustive semantic summary:

- given input X, output must validate against schema Y;
- output file must exist and render without overflow;
- no network writes;
- total provider tokens below N;
- cited values must reconcile to source rows.

This can replace much of demand validation and success specification. It cannot replace the context control plane for provenance, instruction precedence, authorization, freshness, disclosure, or untrusted-content boundaries. It is exceptionally useful when desired behavior is easier to test than to describe.

**Risk:** tests can be incomplete or accidentally tautological. Keep the original utterance and provenance even if tests are the main control representation.

## Alternative E — relational context tables

Store facts, constraints, sources, scopes, freshness, and conflicts in normalized tables and construct task-specific SQL projections.

**Wins:** cheap filters, joins, versioning, indexes, access control, and operational simplicity.

**Loses:** arbitrary nested evidence is less natural; semantic relations require explicit tables.

**Use when:** this is an operational product, not a research knowledge graph.

## Alternative F — event-sourced context

Do not persist a mutable manifest. Persist append-only events—request received, instruction adopted, memory superseded, policy checked, file changed—and derive the current snapshot.

CloudEvents offers a vendor-neutral **wire envelope** in which context attributes can be inspected without decoding the payload, a useful property for routing and policy ([CloudEvents 1.0.2](https://github.com/cloudevents/spec/blob/v1.0.2/cloudevents/spec.md)). It does not provide persistence, ordering, causality, replay, snapshots, correction, or projection semantics; the event store must provide those separately.

**Wins:** exact temporal history, invalidation, replay, auditing, and clean treatment of superseded facts.

**Loses:** snapshot projection and compaction are additional engineering; event meaning must be versioned.

## Alternative G — blackboard architecture

Agents, tools, retrievers, and verifiers read and write a shared structured workspace. Items have confidence, author, authority, dependencies, and status.

**Wins:** natural for asynchronous agents and partial solutions; supports competing hypotheses.

**Loses:** uncontrolled shared state can become a junk drawer; concurrency and truth maintenance are hard. Treat blackboard entries as hypotheses and work items. Accepted facts and decisions should commit to an append-only evidence ledger with provenance and explicit conflict state instead of silently becoming authoritative truth.

## Alternative H — RDF/knowledge graph plus SHACL

Represent facts and their relations as RDF, use ontology terms for meaning, and SHACL shapes for validation. SHACL is a W3C language for validating RDF graphs against shapes ([SHACL Recommendation](https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl/)).

**Wins:** cross-domain interoperability, explicit relationships, flexible schema evolution, rich provenance.

**Loses:** higher tooling and modeling cost; more difficult for ordinary application developers; often unnecessary in a first vertical slice.

## Alternative I — prompt-state summary or model memory

Ask a model to maintain a concise rolling state.

**Wins:** fastest prototype; handles nuance.

**Loses:** lossy, non-deterministic, susceptible to instruction confusion, and hard to reproduce. It should be a derived view, never the sole source of truth.

## Alternative J — human-authored task form or wizard

For costly or high-risk requests, ask the user for typed choices before planning.

**Wins:** turns ambiguity into ground truth; sometimes cheaper than any model cascade.

**Loses:** interaction cost and abandonment; poor for routine requests.

## Recommendation

Implement one `RequestEnvelope` now, with:

- immutable references rather than copied bodies;
- role (`fact`, `instruction`, `preference`, `untrusted_content`, `policy`, `evidence`);
- authority and scope;
- freshness and invalidation keys;
- conflicts and unresolved questions;
- a demand projection;
- acceptance tests;
- a receipt of every lazy resolution.

Split it into a standalone `ContextManifest` service only when multiple hosts, agents, and workflows need independent context snapshots.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Alternatives to `DemandIR`

## What job it is doing

`DemandIR` turns free-form user language into a canonical, model-independent problem statement: required inputs, outputs, effects, qualities, prohibitions, preferences, and success criteria. The important word is *canonical*, not *IR*.

## Alternative A — direct trigger or explicit handle

If the user invokes a known skill, command, primitive, or pack, the handle itself can be the demand. Parameters are validated and execution begins. No semantic IR is necessary.

This should be the first bypass because it deletes interpretation, query generation, retrieval, and route selection.

## Alternative B — intent + slots

Use a closed vocabulary of intents and task-specific slots. This is the lowest-cost general alternative and can be extracted with rules, a classifier, or a tiny model.

**Best for:** repeated product workflows.

**Weakness:** ontology expansion becomes a bottleneck for open-ended work.

## Alternative C — parameterized task template

Map the request to a versioned template with conditions:

``` text
template: analyze_tabular_file@3
if columns contain date -> enable trend branch
if target requested -> enable prediction branch
if output=slides -> attach presentation renderer
```

This is stronger than intent/slots because the template can already contain a validated route skeleton.

## Alternative D — goal + constraints + objective

Represent only what the solver needs:

``` text
initial_types = {csv_blob}
goal_types = {validated_pdf_report}
hard_constraints = {no_external_write, pii_local_only}
soft_objective = 0.5*cost + 0.3*latency + 0.2*risk
```

This avoids narrating the complete problem and maps directly to graph search or optimization.

## Alternative D2 — typed/effect target

Reduce the demand to a compositional target:

``` text
Input × Parameters -> Output ! Effects
```

Add refinements and acceptance tests only where the base types are insufficient. This turns route discovery into a type/effect inhabitation problem and is often the most useful lightweight replacement for a broad semantic IR.

## Alternative E — examples or tests

Use input/output pairs, golden files, schemas, properties, and negative examples. A synthesizer or route solver finds a composition satisfying them.

**Best for:** transformation, code, extraction, and formatting tasks.

**Weakness:** examples may under-specify safety, authorization, or non-functional goals.

## Alternative F — program sketch

The demand is a partial plan with holes:

``` text
read(file) -> [table_cleaner?] -> aggregate(by=region) -> [chart?] -> pdf
```

Retrieval fills only the holes. This can be created deterministically from a UI, previous recipe, or a model.

**Wins:** dramatically narrows search; makes user intent inspectable.

## Alternative G — structured query plan

Skip a separate demand representation and emit a `QueryPlan` containing must-have types, effects, lexical terms, standards, exclusions, and fallback policy. The retrieval plan becomes the canonical interpretation.

**Tradeoff:** it couples intent to the current index and retrieval engine; later backends may need reinterpretation.

## Alternative H — PDDL/HTN planning problem

Represent state, actions, predicates, and goals in a planning language. PDDL separates domain actions from problem instances and supports preconditions and effects ([original PDDL report](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/dvm/papers/pddl.pdf)). Hierarchical task networks add task decompositions.

**Wins:** principled planning, explicit state transitions, mature algorithms.

**Loses:** encoding real software effects, data schemas, uncertainty, and rich preferences is laborious. PDDL standardizes domain/problem inputs, not a universal executable workflow format; concrete bindings, runtime errors, credentials, and receipts still need a lowering layer.

## Alternative I — CSP, CP-SAT, SMT, or ILP model

Compile requirements directly into decision variables and constraints. OR-Tools CP-SAT provides exact feasible/optimal/infeasible statuses for integer constraint models ([CP-SAT documentation](https://developers.google.com/optimization/cp/cp_solver)); Z3 supports satisfiability modulo theories for richer logical constraints ([Z3 Guide](https://microsoft.github.io/z3guide/docs/logic/intro/)).

**Wins:** global constraints, formal feasibility status, and exact optimization inside the encoding/bounds. Human-useful infeasibility explanations require tracked assumptions and an explanation layer.

**Loses:** semantic intent still has to become correct formulas; nonlinear runtime behavior may not fit.

## Alternative J — generated natural-language specification

Let an LLM rewrite the request into a compact specification.

**Wins:** broad coverage and easy prototyping.

**Loses:** it is not reliably canonical, typed, or complete. Use a schema-constrained output and validate it; keep uncertainty rather than forcing false precision.

## Alternative K — no fixed demand; interactive hypothesis set

Maintain several interpretations with probabilities and retrieve routes that discriminate among them. Ask the user only if the route or effect differs materially.

**Wins:** avoids premature commitment.

**Loses:** branching state and evaluation become more complex.

## Recommendation

Start with a small schema containing:

``` text
goal_family
known_inputs / required_outputs
hard_constraints / soft_preferences
allowed_effects / prohibited_effects
acceptance_tests
uncertain_fields with confidence and alternatives
original_request_ref
```

Support three bypasses before constructing it fully: an explicit sealed handle, an exact content digest, or a host-triggered approved template. A canonical/semantic historical match may skip open-ended interpretation, but it must still extract and revalidate every safety-relevant constraint, environment, policy, authorization, effect, and oracle. Later, compile the same demand projection into graph predicates, SQL filters, or solver constraints. Do not require a model to populate fields that are irrelevant to the active task family.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. Alternatives to a verified `PrimitiveCard`

## What job it is doing

A `PrimitiveCard` is a compact capability projection used for discovery and composition without exposing full code. “Verified” should mean that its claims are tied to evidence—not merely that an LLM wrote a plausible summary.

One object rarely serves all consumers optimally. Consider four projections over one versioned primitive record:

1.  **Retrieval view:** aliases, examples, standards, error vocabulary, domain terms.
2.  **Solver view:** typed ports, preconditions, effects, qualities, resources.
3.  **Selector view:** route-relevant differentiators and evidence.
4.  **Execution view:** immutable body reference, runtime requirements, required capability/secret classes, sandbox profile, and digest. Request-scoped credentials or capability handles are resolved separately and never projected to a selector.

## Alternative A — signature and docstring only

Use the existing function signature, type hints, and documentation.

**Wins:** almost zero authoring cost.

**Loses:** effects, operational requirements, behavioral guarantees, security, compatibility, and evidence are often absent or stale.

**Use when:** primitives are internal, simple, pure, and tested.

## Alternative B — OpenAPI or tool/function schema

Describe callable operations with standard request/response schemas. OpenAPI provides a language-agnostic interface description for HTTP APIs ([OpenAPI Specification](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html)). MCP/tool schemas or JSON Schema function definitions fill a similar role for agent tools.

**Wins:** existing tooling, code generation, validators, and ecosystem compatibility.

**Loses:** multi-step semantics, non-HTTP functions, nuanced effects, cost, trust, and behavioral evidence need extensions.

## Alternative C — IDL record

Use Protobuf, Avro, Thrift, or another interface definition language for ports, messages, and versioning.

**Wins:** precise wire types and cross-language generation.

**Loses:** discoverability and semantic capability description remain separate.

## Alternative D — design-by-contract

Specify preconditions, postconditions, invariants, frame conditions, exceptions, and effects.

**Wins:** much stronger solver and verifier semantics than descriptive cards.

**Loses:** authoring and proof burden; many useful properties cannot be decided statically.

## Alternative E — property/test-backed behavioral fingerprint

Index examples, property tests, failure signatures, normalized outputs, effect probes, and benchmark results. Discovery is based on demonstrated behavior.

**Wins:** evidence can reveal misleading descriptions and distinguish near-duplicates.

**Loses:** test coverage is finite; executing probes may be expensive or unsafe.

## Alternative F — source-derived descriptor

Extract AST symbols, imports, call graph, types, docstrings, tests, licenses, SBOM, and static-analysis findings automatically. An LLM may summarize this evidence, but the evidence remains addressable.

**Wins:** scalable ingestion and lower manual burden.

**Loses:** static evidence does not fully describe runtime behavior; summaries can drift after code changes unless digest-bound.

## Alternative G — capability tags or ontology terms

Represent each primitive using controlled concepts such as `parse/pdf`, `effect/network-read`, `standard/iso-8601`, `quality/lossless`.

**Wins:** extremely compact, deterministic filtering.

**Loses:** tag governance, granularity, and synonym coverage become a product of their own.

## Alternative H — component/package manifest

Treat the primitive as an installable artifact with dependencies, entry point, permissions, version, platform, SBOM, and provenance. OCI standardizes image manifests and content-addressable layers ([OCI Image Specification](https://specs.opencontainers.org/image-spec/)).

**Wins:** deployability and supply-chain integrity.

**Loses:** interface and semantic behavior still need another contract.

## Alternative I — WebAssembly component contract

Compile primitives to Wasm components with typed interfaces. The Component Model is designed for interoperable Wasm components with well-defined APIs ([WebAssembly Component Model](https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/)). WIT/component contracts describe types, not behavior, trust, effects, or authorization; isolation depends on host imports, WASI/runtime policy, and behavioral verification.

**Wins:** language-neutral composition and strong sandboxing potential.

**Loses:** ecosystem maturity, host capability design, and conversion cost.

## Alternative J — entire solution pack

Describe and verify a complete route or workflow rather than each atomic primitive. Retrieve the pack first; inspect internals only for adaptation.

**Wins:** highest reuse and lowest planning token cost.

**Loses:** combinatorial pack catalog; less flexible than primitive composition.

## Alternative K — embedding only

Embed source, docs, examples, or traces and search semantically without a formal card.

**Wins:** rapid ingestion and high recall for paraphrases.

**Loses:** no safe type/effect composition, weak explanations, and poor guarantees. Embeddings are a retrieval feature, not a contract.

## What “verified” can mean

Verification strength should be explicit:

| Evidence level         | Meaning                                        |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `declared`             | Author or model stated the claim               |
| `schema_checked`       | Descriptor validates structurally              |
| `statically_derived`   | Type/AST/package evidence supports it          |
| `example_passed`       | Named example passed on this digest            |
| `property_tested`      | Generated cases satisfied properties           |
| `sandbox_observed`     | Effects and outputs were observed safely       |
| `externally_certified` | Independent validator/certification attests it |
| `formally_proved`      | Machine-checkable proof covers the claim       |

Never collapse these into one boolean `verified=true`. The rows are not one total ladder: a supply-chain attestation, production canary, integration test, and formal proof cover different properties. Store property-scoped evidence tuples such as `(claim, artifact_digest, environment, verifier_version, time, result)` and compare evidence only within the relevant claim.

## Recommendation

Use a standard interface schema plus a small Taedri extension for effects, resources, policy, examples, and evidence. Keep immutable, digest-bound interface/body identity separate from append-only or scoped telemetry, lifecycle, authorization, policy eligibility, and verification evidence. Generate compact projections from those authoritative planes. A custom `PrimitiveCard` should be a view, not the only source of truth.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Alternatives to a port-level hypergraph

## What job it is doing

The graph represents which primitive ports can satisfy which other ports, including multi-input requirements, alternatives, effects, resources, adapters, and route-level constraints. A hyperedge is valuable when one relation naturally connects multiple inputs and outputs. It is not automatically the best persistence or query model.

## Alternative A — no graph

Retrieve a complete pack, template, or primitive; ask code or a model to connect the rest.

**Wins:** simplest prototype.

**Loses:** weak completeness, repeated planning, and no deterministic compatibility proof.

## Alternative B — relational tables

Store `primitive`, `port`, `type`, `effect`, `compatibility`, and `adapter` tables. Use joins and recursive common table expressions for route search.

**Wins:** mature operations, indexes, constraints, transactions, and easy filtering.

**Loses:** path and hyperedge queries can be verbose; recursive optimization varies by database.

**Best first-slice choice:** yes, including very large catalogs when indexes and blocking select a small request-local subproblem. What should not scale globally is recursive full-catalog traversal or materialized pairwise compatibility.

## Alternative C — bipartite port graph

Use two node classes—primitive invocations and values/ports—with ordinary edges. An n-ary primitive becomes one invocation node connected to all required inputs and outputs.

**Wins:** represents hypergraph semantics using conventional graph engines; natural dataflow view.

**Loses:** more nodes and hops; global constraints still live outside the graph.

Keep catalog and execution levels distinct. A catalog graph contains operation definitions plus port/type/schema nodes. A request-local plan contains invocation instances plus concrete artifact, state, resource, and authority values. Reusing catalog nodes as runtime values can accidentally leak bindings or state across executions.

## Alternative D — property graph

Model primitives, ports, types, standards, policies, and evidence as nodes/edges with properties.

**Wins:** intuitive traversal and diagnostics; common graph tooling.

**Loses:** exact semantics of n-ary relations and validation depend on application conventions.

## Alternative E — dataflow DAG catalog

Store only known valid workflows and subgraphs rather than the full compatibility universe.

**Wins:** smaller, higher precision, easier execution.

**Loses:** weak novel composition; catalog coverage is the bottleneck.

## Alternative F — AND/OR graph

OR nodes represent alternative ways to satisfy a need; AND nodes represent requirements that must all be satisfied.

**Wins:** directly expresses alternatives versus bundles and supports dynamic programming.

**Loses:** effects, state, and cycles require careful semantics.

## Alternative G — factor graph or constraint network

Variables represent route choices; factors score or constrain compatibility, cost, policy, and quality.

**Wins:** supports global tradeoffs and uncertain evidence.

**Loses:** inference/optimization machinery is heavier than path search.

## Alternative H — RDF/OWL plus SHACL

Use semantic relations for types and capabilities, inference for subsumption, and shapes for constraints.

**Wins:** ontology interoperability and reasoning across heterogeneous registries.

**Loses:** operational complexity and open-world semantics may surprise application engineers.

## Alternative I — Petri net

Places represent conditions/resources, transitions represent primitive actions, and tokens represent state.

**Wins:** concurrency, synchronization, resource consumption, and reachability are first-class.

**Loses:** data payload types and rich cost objectives require extensions; state-space explosion.

## Alternative J — state machine/statechart

Represent legal state transitions rather than typed data connections.

**Wins:** long-running interactive and lifecycle workflows.

**Loses:** awkward for arbitrary data transformation pipelines.

## Alternative K — session types/process algebra

Describe legal communication protocols between components.

**Wins:** formal guarantees for concurrent message exchanges.

**Loses:** specialized expertise and tooling; excessive for ordinary tool chains.

## Alternative L — on-demand compatibility computation

Do not materialize all edges. Retrieve possible primitives, then call a type unifier, schema matcher, adapter registry, or probe to compute edges locally.

**Wins:** avoids quadratic edge storage and stale compatibility.

**Loses:** more per-request compute; exact reproducibility requires recording the compatibility function version.

At 5M–40M primitives, this is more than an implementation detail. A full pairwise compatibility graph can be physically infeasible even when the logical problem is hypergraphic. The scalable pattern is:

``` text
type/capability/effect indexes
  -> eligible producer and consumer blocks
  -> lazy compatibility predicates and adapter lookup
  -> request-local operation/value graph
  -> cache only proven edges and successful subgraphs
```

The physical store can therefore remain relational and inverted-indexed while the solver receives an exact logical hypergraph for the small relevant subproblem.

Compatibility edges also need explicit evidence classes:

- exact type/schema identity;
- proved subtype/refinement compatibility;
- verified lossless adapter;
- explicitly permitted lossy adapter;
- empirical compatibility from bounded probes;
- semantic candidate requiring further proof.

Semantic similarity and probes may generate or rank edge hypotheses, but they must not silently turn into executable edges.

## Recommendation

Persist normalized primitive and port records plus explicit adapters. Compute a request-local bipartite/hypergraph projection after retrieval. Materialize only high-value compatibility edges and successful subgraphs. Adopt a dedicated hypergraph store only if benchmarks show that n-ary composition and global traversal dominate latency or correctness.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Alternatives to `GraphIR`

## What job it is doing

`GraphIR` is the selected, executable composition after retrieval and planning. Its value is decoupling selection from execution and allowing validation, optimization, display, caching, and lowering into one or more runtimes.

## Alternative A — direct pack invocation

If a known solution pack is selected, bind parameters and invoke its precompiled execution representation. No new graph is constructed per request, but replay must still revalidate artifact closure, policy, environment, capability bindings, lifecycle, and oracle validity.

## Alternative B — ordered recipe

Represent a linear chain such as `A > B > C` with bindings and versions.

**Wins:** tiny and readable.

**Loses:** weak branching, parallelism, joins, loops, retries, compensation, and human steps.

## Alternative C — minimal DAG JSON/YAML

Use nodes, typed bindings, conditions, and outputs. Keep execution semantics deliberately small.

**Wins:** sufficient for most initial data/tool composition; easy to hash and validate.

**Loses:** every added control-flow construct risks creating a new workflow language.

## Alternative D — generated Python/TypeScript

Emit ordinary code that imports or invokes primitives.

**Wins:** existing language semantics, debuggers, tests, and libraries.

**Loses:** harder static policy analysis; code injection and sandboxing risk; canonical equivalence and caching are difficult.

## Alternative E — shell/Make/Snakemake/Nextflow

Use established build or scientific workflow representations.

**Wins:** mature dependency execution for files and batch jobs.

**Loses:** not ideal for typed service interactions, long-lived state, or privileged agent tools.

## Alternative F — CWL or WDL

Common Workflow Language describes portable command-line workflows, including typed inputs/outputs, dependencies, scattering, and conditions ([CWL Workflow specification](https://www.commonwl.org/v1.2/Workflow.html)).

**Wins:** vendor-neutral portability and existing runners.

**Loses:** primarily batch/data workflow semantics; interactive services and compensating transactions are less natural.

## Alternative G — Temporal workflow

Lower the plan into a durable workflow platform. Temporal workflows provide resilient execution semantics for long-running application logic ([Temporal workflow documentation](https://docs.temporal.io/workflows)).

**Wins:** retries, durable state, timers, signals, and recovery.

**Loses:** SDK/runtime commitment and deterministic workflow constraints.

## Alternative H — AWS States Language / Step Functions

Emit a state-machine definition in Amazon States Language ([ASL specification](https://states-language.net/spec.html)).

**Wins:** managed orchestration and clear operational tooling.

**Loses:** cloud coupling, service limits, and potentially awkward local/private execution.

## Alternative I — Argo/Airflow/Dagster/Prefect

Lower into an existing orchestration framework suited to the deployment environment.

**Wins:** scheduling, retries, visibility, integrations.

**Loses:** each platform imposes its own runtime and graph semantics.

## Alternative J — BPMN

Use a business-process model for tasks, gateways, messages, timers, and human work. BPMN is standardized by OMG ([BPMN 2.0.2](https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0.2/PDF)).

**Wins:** human-readable business processes and human-in-the-loop steps.

**Loses:** verbose for low-level data composition; engine behavior and extensions vary.

## Alternative K — PDDL/HTN plan

Keep the planner’s action sequence/decomposition as the execution plan.

**Wins:** no translation between planner and IR.

**Loses:** runtime error handling, concrete data bindings, credentials, and observability need another layer.

## Alternative L — Petri net/statechart

Use formal transition semantics directly, especially for concurrency and long-lived process state.

## Alternative M — compiler IR

Treat compositions as programs and lower them through a control-flow, SSA, or multi-level compiler IR.

**Wins:** mature validation and optimization techniques, explicit values/control, and multiple backend lowerings.

**Loses:** considerable compiler engineering and operational-effect dialect design; premature unless route volumes and multiple runtimes justify it.

## Alternative N — e-graph/equality saturation optimizer

Start from valid plans, represent many equivalent rewrites compactly, and extract the lowest-cost form.

**Wins:** powerful optimization of known-equivalent compositions.

**Loses:** an e-graph is an optimization data structure, not normally an executable plan replacement. Rewrites must be effect-aware and justified; ordinary algebraic equality can be invalid for stateful, nondeterministic, authorized, or externally visible operations.

## Alternative O — typed combinator `PlanAST`

Represent plans as a small algebra—`seq`, `parallel`, `branch`, `map`, `join`, `retry`, `approve`, and `compensate`—with typed children and effect annotations.

**Wins:** more compact and model-friendly than a generic node/edge graph; compiler-friendly; invalid compositions can be rejected while constructing the tree.

**Loses:** shared subgraphs, arbitrary cycles, and runtime-specific behavior need explicit extensions or lowering rules.

## Alternative P — specialized plan family instead of one universal IR

Lower a high-level plan into the representation that matches its semantics:

``` text
PlanAST
  -> BatchDAG
  -> ReactiveStateMachine
  -> HumanProcess
  -> DurableWorkflow
  -> LocalCodeAST
```

This avoids a universal `GraphIR` that either grows into an entire programming language or silently underspecifies backend behavior.

## Recommendation

Define the smallest canonical high-level `PlanAST` needed for validation and hashing, then lower shared subexpressions to an identity-bearing DAG:

- immutable primitive/version references;
- typed bindings;
- conditions and bounded fan-out;
- effect and authority declarations;
- retry/timeout/idempotency policy references;
- oracle references;
- lowering target.

Then lower it to an existing runtime-specific representation. Every lowering needs semantic-preservation/conformance tests and must reject unsupported retry, compensation, concurrency, authority, or effect semantics instead of approximating them. Do not build a general orchestration engine as part of the retrieval vertical slice.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 6. Alternatives to exact lookup

Exact lookup deserves its own decision because it is not a retrieval algorithm in the usual sense; it is a bypass.

## Alternatives

- **Explicit primitive/pack handle:** user or host supplies a stable identifier.
- **Content digest:** resolve an immutable descriptor or recipe by hash.
- **Canonical alias table:** normalized command, standard, error code, MIME type, file extension, or package coordinate maps to a handle.
- **Database predicate lookup:** exact fields such as input schema ID, output schema ID, tenant, environment, and lifecycle.
- **AST/import/symbol trigger:** changed symbol or referenced API deterministically selects a primitive or hook.
- **Rule-engine trigger:** a declarative condition selects a pack.
- **Signed registry resolution:** identifier plus trust policy resolves only an approved version.
- **No exact stage:** send everything to search; simpler but wastes latency and tokens and loses deterministic replay.

## Recommendation

Keep exact lookup. Expand “exact” beyond string equality to include stable handles, digests, typed IDs, schema IDs, standards, tool triggers, and canonical task fingerprints. Revalidate authorization and lifecycle even on a hit.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 7. Alternatives to historical reuse

## Alternative A — no history

Every request is solved from current registry state.

**Wins:** no stale-route or privacy risk; simplest evaluation baseline.

**Loses:** repeated work and no learning.

## Alternative B — exact recipe cache

Map a canonical demand fingerprint to a bound, previously verified plan.

**Wins:** largest normal-path savings; deterministic.

**Loses:** low recall unless fingerprints normalize irrelevant variation.

## Alternative C — semantic cache

Retrieve prior demands or plans by embedding or sparse similarity.

**Wins:** paraphrase reuse.

**Loses:** a similar prompt can have a decisive different constraint. Treat it as a candidate, not an automatic hit.

## Alternative D — parameterized route templates

Mine common plans and replace concrete inputs with typed variables and guards.

**Wins:** generalizes safely across repeated families.

**Loses:** template induction and guard correctness require verification.

## Alternative E — frequent subgraph/macros

Cache common route fragments rather than complete routes.

**Wins:** compositional reuse even when endpoints differ.

**Loses:** fragment boundaries and interface quality matter.

## Alternative F — success prior

History only influences ranking: per tenant, environment, task family, primitive version, and route record success, latency, cost, and failure modes.

**Wins:** less brittle than direct replay.

**Loses:** feedback loops can entrench incumbents and hide new superior primitives. Raw success rates are observationally biased because only selected/executed routes receive outcomes. Log exposure/selection propensity, use shrinkage and cold-start handling, and explore only among already feasible/safe routes.

## Alternative G — contextual bandit

Learn which retrieval, selector, or route arm wins under observed context while preserving exploration.

**Wins:** online adaptation.

**Loses:** delayed/biased rewards, safety constraints, non-stationarity, and audit complexity.

## Alternative H — case-based reasoning

Retrieve the prior problem, explanation, adaptations, and verified outcome; explicitly transform it to the new case.

## Recommendation

Use a hierarchy: exact verified plan → guarded parameterized template → successful subgraph → history prior. All reuse must be keyed by primitive digests, environment, policy snapshot, verifier version, and relevant demand constraints. Include a stateless arm to expose stale-history regressions.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 8. Alternatives to fielded BM25

## What fielded BM25 is good at

Lexical signals in names, types, aliases, standards, errors, examples, and descriptions often identify software capabilities more precisely than generic dense semantics. Field weighting prevents a verbose description from overpowering an exact port type or standard identifier.

## Alternatives

### A. Structured filters only

Use SQL/bitmap indexes over types, effects, standards, environment, trust, and lifecycle.

**Best when:** descriptors are complete and demand parsing is reliable.

### B. TF-IDF/vector-space retrieval

Simpler lexical baseline. Useful for ablations, though BM25’s term-frequency saturation and length normalization usually make it a stronger default.

### C. Query-likelihood or divergence-from-randomness models

Classical probabilistic lexical alternatives available in mature search engines.

### D. trigram, edit-distance, and phonetic matching

Good for misspelled identifiers, API names, file types, and product vocabulary. This is complementary to, not a full replacement for, semantic retrieval.

### E. SQLite FTS5 or database-native full-text search

A deployment alternative to operating Lucene/OpenSearch. SQLite FTS5 supports phrases, prefixes, proximity, column filters, tokenizers, and a built-in `bm25()` function, making it excellent for an embedded first slice ([SQLite FTS5](https://sqlite.org/fts5.html)).

### F. learned sparse retrieval

Models such as SPLADE expand terms while retaining sparse inverted-index retrieval.

**Wins:** paraphrase recall with inspectable sparse terms.

**Loses:** model inference and domain training; expanded terms can create false matches.

### G. dense single-vector ANN

Embed each primitive/view and demand; retrieve nearest neighbors.

**Wins:** semantic paraphrases and multilingual matching.

**Loses:** exact identifiers and negation can be weak; vector index and model versioning; no typed compatibility proof.

### H. multi-vector/late-interaction retrieval

Represent documents with token-level vectors and score fine-grained interactions.

**Wins:** better matching of distinct fields and rare terms than one vector.

**Loses:** larger index and compute cost.

### I. local cross-encoder reranking

Retrieve broadly by lexical/dense methods, then jointly score demand and candidate text.

**Wins:** often more accurate than independent embeddings; non-generative and provider-token-free when local.

**Loses:** scales only across a bounded candidate set and still consumes tokenized inference, accelerator/device time, energy, memory, and latency. Measure device-seconds or FLOPs rather than calling it free.

### J. behavioral retrieval

Match tests, examples, error traces, effects, schema transformations, or safe probe outputs.

**Wins:** finds what the primitive does, not what it is called.

**Loses:** evidence generation and storage cost.

### K. code-aware retrieval

Use symbols, AST, imports, types, call graph, package coordinates, and tests.

### L. graph-neighborhood retrieval

Seed exact types or known primitives and expand adapters, compatible neighbors, and successful route fragments.

### M. LSH/MinHash/SimHash blocking

Use cheap modality-specific approximate similarity to collapse duplicates or form candidate blocks before expensive scoring. It normally runs before costly ranking, not as a generic later semantic-recall upgrade.

**Best use:** deduplication and broad blocking, not final semantic ranking. A hard block can destroy recall, so measure blocking recall separately and retain a bypass/union path.

### N. federated fusion

Run lexical, dense, behavioral, history, and graph retrievers and fuse ranks using reciprocal-rank fusion, learned-to-rank, or calibrated scores.

Do not max-normalize every signal and add fixed weights as the only baseline. A uniformly weak retriever can still receive its full assigned weight. Better alternatives are:

- apply authorization, lifecycle, type, effect, and environment gates before relevance ranking;
- use reciprocal-rank fusion when score scales are incomparable;
- calibrate each signal against held-out relevance/route labels when enough data exists;
- train a lightweight learning-to-rank model after clean outcome receipts accumulate;
- preserve a Pareto frontier when cost, risk, latency, and privacy cannot honestly be reduced to one scalar.

Distinguish **parallel candidate generation** from **waterfall escalation**. Exact/alias, lexical, trigram, history, graph, sparse, and dense generators may run in one cheap parallel tier and contribute a recall-safe union. Expensive cross-encoding, model-written queries, deeper graph expansion, and external calls belong in sequential escalation. A strict one-after-another waterfall can add latency and prevent useful fusion.

### O. LLM-written query

Use a model to generate structured or natural-language queries only after cheaper paths fail.

**Wins:** can infer unstated synonyms and query strategy.

**Loses:** provider tokens, latency, variability, query hallucination, and an extra correctness surface.

## Recommendation

Do not replace fielded BM25 with one fashionable retriever. Benchmark a modular hybrid:

1.  structured filters and exact terms;
2.  embedded lexical BM25/FTS;
3.  aliases, trigram, and LSH blocking;
4.  optional learned sparse or dense recall;
5.  local cross-encoder reranking;
6.  graph and history signals;
7.  hosted query generation only on measured misses.

Fielded BM25 remains the cheapest high-quality baseline, but SQLite FTS5 may be a better deployment choice than a separate search cluster for the first slice.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 9. Alternatives to typed bidirectional route solving

## Alternative A — pack/template match

Retrieve a complete verified route and bind it. This is preferable to search whenever available.

## Alternative B — forward chaining/BFS
