
## 14. Test and evaluation program

### Contract and identity tests

- canonicalization golden files across languages, Unicode, paths, namespaces, schemas, and version intervals;
- deterministic ID/fingerprint reproduction across process order and machines;
- schema forward/backward compatibility and unknown-field preservation;
- hash collision defense by comparing stored canonical keys;
- n-ary relation projections round-trip to the same canonical relation.

### Compatibility solver tests

- one table-driven suite for every axis and verdict;
- directionality, symmetry only where declared, subtyping variance, generic constraints, nullability, units, cardinality, protocols, async/stream, ownership, effects, errors, policy, and version intervals;
- adapter conversion, introduced effects, lossiness, and multi-hop dominance;
- minimal unsat-core correctness;
- unknown evidence never converted into a false hard fail;
- contradictory evidence retained and surfaced.

### Candidate generation tests

- gold compatible/non-compatible pair corpus with hard negatives;
- blocking recall and reduction ratio by task/edge family;
- exact, BM25, LSH, ANN, graph, and fusion ablations;
- adversarial same-name/different-semantics and different-name/same-contract pairs;
- unknown-field and dynamic-language cases;
- no quadratic behavior: bound candidate visits, pair solves, allocations, and wall time as corpus grows;
- tenant/ACL candidates excluded before scoring or graph expansion.

### Fingerprint tests

- exact canonical digest sensitivity/invariance properties;
- MinHash/SimHash empirical collision and recall curves;
- clone fingerprint stability under formatting/renaming and sensitivity to behavior changes;
- ANN recall@k under quantization and model upgrades;
- graph-fingerprint stability for irrelevant local edits and invalidation for relevant topology edits.

### Versioning and invalidation tests

- source, build flag, dependency, policy, adapter, evidence, model, and graph-topology changes each invalidate exactly the required derived records;
- stale cache never survives a mismatched signature/policy/adapter epoch;
- negative cache is cleared when missing coverage becomes available;
- branch/workspace overlays do not mutate base-epoch truth;
- interrupted publication never exposes a partial epoch.

### Route and end-to-end tests

- direct connection, one adapter, bounded multi-adapter, no route, ambiguous route, and cycle cases;
- bidirectional solver agrees with exhaustive search on small fixtures;
- dominance pruning never removes the only policy-valid route;
- body resolution occurs only after selection;
- selected route executes in sandbox and passes independent oracle;
- exact receipt can reproduce candidate/assessment versions and explain exclusions.

### Property, fuzz, and load tests

- fuzz schemas, types, ranges, Unicode, corrupted bundles, malformed evidence, and graph deltas;
- property: adding a true hard constraint cannot increase the eligible direct-candidate set;
- property: adding low-authority unknown evidence cannot create hard incompatibility;
- property: exact verified replay outranks semantically similar unverified alternatives under the same policy;
- sustained indexing/update/query concurrency, p50/p95/p99 latency, memory, index size, and recovery tests.

### Required metrics

- compatible-pair recall after blocking;
- candidates generated and pair solves per query;
- direct/adapter/unknown/incompatible precision and recall;
- false-confident compatibility rate;
- no-match abstention quality;
- route success under independent oracle;
- incremental recall and cost of each waterfall stage;
- cache/materialization hit rate and stale-hit rate;
- tokens, local compute, latency, and total cost per verified successful route;
- index bytes per port/explicit edge and update amplification;
- evidence coverage and contradiction rates.

Use exhaustive all-pairs solving only on small benchmark shards to create an oracle for measuring block recall. At production scale, retain a randomized audit stream from blocked-out pairs to estimate hidden false negatives.

## 15. First vertical slice

1.  Implement contracts for `CompatibilitySignature`, `EdgeAssertion`, `EdgeFeatureBundle`, `CompatibilityAssessment`, and `EdgeSearchReceipt`.
2.  Extract Python function/method parameter, return, exception, import, effect, and test edges from the PyPI/workspace slice.
3.  Build exact type/schema/effect fingerprints, fielded BM25, MinHash/SimHash, one semantic vector per input/output meaning, and typed one-hop graph fingerprints.
4.  Build Roaring-bitmap blocks for direction, port role, type head/ancestor, semantic role, cardinality, temporal mode, runtime, effect, trust zone, and unknown buckets.
5.  Implement direct deterministic pair solving for the 24 axes with explicit `unknown` and one-hop adapter lookup.
6.  Ship `edge.search_assertions`, `edge.compatible_from`, `edge.assess_pair`, `edge.find_adapter`, and bounded `edge.route` through CLI and MCP.
7.  Materialize only exact verified edges and accepted route history; keep other assessments in dependency-keyed cache.
8.  Benchmark exact-only, typed block, BM25, LSH, embedding, graph, fusion, deterministic solver, local ranker, and optional model arms.
9.  Gate launch on high blocking recall, low false-confident compatibility, correct abstention, sublinear candidate visits, reproducible receipts, and independently verified route success.

The subsystem succeeds when an agent can ask “what existing output can safely feed this input?” or “what verified route connects these boundaries?” and receive a small, typed, evidence-backed answer without an LLM reading the corpus or the platform enumerating every possible edge.

# Searchable Code-Graph Edges: Primary Research, Failure Boundaries, and Implementation Recommendations

> **ANNEX STATUS — RESEARCH AND RECOMMENDATIONS.** External research supports design
> choices; it is not empirical proof that the corresponding Taedri components are
> implemented or production-ready.

**Prepared:** 2026-07-15
**Scope:** Existing-code ingestion, similarity blocking, graph-edge retrieval, code embeddings, typed API compatibility, and hybrid search for a language-neutral code entity graph.
**Source policy:** Foundational papers, standards, specifications, official project documentation, and first-party model/benchmark reports. Broad secondary explainers were intentionally excluded.

## Executive recommendation

Do not build one universal “code similarity” score. Existing code has several kinds of sameness that are useful for different jobs but are not interchangeable:

- **Byte/content identity** answers whether an exact artifact was seen before.
- **Lexical overlap** finds copied or lightly edited implementations.
- **Weighted-feature similarity** finds near-duplicates after identifiers and common syntax are down-weighted.
- **Local graph similarity** finds entities with similar typed neighborhoods or control/data-flow shapes.
- **Motif similarity** finds repeated architectural patterns.
- **Semantic embedding similarity** finds code serving a similar human purpose despite different words or structure.
- **Type compatibility** answers whether one output can legally feed another input.
- **Behavioral evidence** answers whether the composed result actually works.

Those questions require an **orthogonal fingerprint bundle**, followed by exact gates and verification. A practical retrieval waterfall is:

1.  Resolve exact entity IDs, package/release coordinates, content hashes, symbol paths, and signatures.
2.  Apply hard filters for language/runtime, version, license/policy, availability, modality, and effect constraints.
3.  Search fielded lexical indexes for names, signatures, docstrings, types, exceptions, examples, and package metadata.
4.  Search MinHash/weighted-MinHash and SimHash lanes for near-duplicate candidates.
5.  Search typed neighborhood, path, motif, and Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) fingerprint lanes.
6.  Search sparse and dense semantic representations, selectively adding late interaction.
7.  Fuse candidate rankings, initially with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).
8.  Run a typed, directional compatibility solver; reject incompatible candidates or insert verified adapters.
9.  Resolve bodies only for finalists, execute in a controlled environment, and verify independently.
10. Record exact inputs, index epochs, fingerprint generators, candidate sets, thresholds, route decisions, and evidence in a receipt.

The central rule is:

> **Fingerprints and embeddings propose; contracts, policy, and evidence dispose.**

## Technique placement matrix

| Technique                                         | Native representation / metric                               | Good use                                                     | Do not use as                                                  | Recommended role                                    |
|---------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| SHA-256 or another versioned cryptographic digest | Exact bytes or canonical serialization                       | Integrity, exact cache, immutable artifact identity          | Semantic equivalence, rename-stable identity                   | First lookup and provenance anchor                  |
| MinHash                                           | Set Jaccard similarity                                       | Token/AST/edge/path shingle overlap; near-duplicate blocking | Order-sensitive comparison, weighted counts, type proof        | Cheap candidate generator followed by exact Jaccard |
| Consistent weighted sampling / weighted MinHash   | Generalized Jaccard on nonnegative weighted features         | Typed-edge counts, IDF-weighted tokens, motif histograms     | Signed features, behavior, compatibility                       | Candidate generator for weighted multisets          |
| SimHash / random-hyperplane LSH                   | Angular/cosine similarity estimated by Hamming distance      | Compact weighted lexical or structural fingerprints          | Exact identity, Jaccard estimator, semantic correctness        | Very compact secondary blocker                      |
| WL neighborhood fingerprints                      | Iteratively refined labeled neighborhoods                    | Rename-tolerant local structural retrieval                   | Graph-isomorphism proof, global behavior proof                 | Multi-radius structural lane                        |
| Graphlet/motif counts                             | Small subgraph count or sample vector                        | Architectural role and repeated-pattern retrieval            | Precise ordering, long-range dependency semantics              | Coarse graph-shape feature lane                     |
| Path/walk shingles                                | Bounded typed paths and traces                               | Call-chain, data-flow, effect-flow, and workflow similarity  | Whole-graph equivalence                                        | MinHash/BM25 features and route hints               |
| Sparse learned retrieval                          | Learned term expansion in an inverted index                  | Vocabulary mismatch while retaining inspectable terms        | Type or safety validation                                      | Optional first-stage semantic lane                  |
| Dense code embeddings                             | Cosine/dot-product in learned space                          | Natural-language-to-code and cross-lingual semantic recall   | Identity, compatibility, quality, license, or security verdict | Recall lane, never the final gate                   |
| Late interaction / multivectors                   | Token/facet-level maximum similarity                         | Final semantic ranking when a single vector blurs details    | First lookup across the entire corpus without cost controls    | Rerank a bounded candidate set                      |
| Typed compatibility solver                        | Directional assignability plus effects and versions          | Deterministic composition and adapter discovery              | Semantic discovery from vague intent                           | Hard post-retrieval gate                            |
| Runtime/static verification                       | Tests, schemas, analyzers, traces, formal or property checks | Behavioral acceptance and learned feedback                   | Cheap corpus-wide first-stage retrieval                        | Final acceptance and evidence                       |

## 1. Exact hashes and content addressing

Cryptographic hashes and similarity hashes solve opposite problems. A cryptographic hash should make even a tiny change produce an unrelated digest; locality-sensitive methods deliberately make similar items collide or remain close.

The [NIST Secure Hash Standard](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final) defines SHA-family digests for detecting whether messages changed. [Git's object model](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Internals-Git-Objects) demonstrates content-addressed blobs and trees, while the [Software Heritage persistent identifier specification](https://www.swhid.org/specification/v1.1/) defines identifiers for archived source-code objects.

### Use exact hashes for

- Byte-identical files, distributions, source archives, generated index segments, and serialized cards.
- Idempotent ingestion and exact-result caches.
- Evidence receipts that must bind to the exact body, schema, compiler, extraction tool, and graph snapshot.
- Merkle-style invalidation: when a child entity changes, recompute only affected parent summaries.

### Do not use exact hashes for

- Logical identity across revisions.
- Alpha-renamed or reformatted code.
- Equivalent APIs implemented in different languages.
- Proof that two programs behave the same.

### Recommended identity split

Keep at least three distinct identifiers:

1.  `occurrence_id`: where an entity occurred in an exact source snapshot.
2.  `content_id`: digest of the exact or explicitly normalized content.
3.  `logical_entity_id`: a lineage/family identity maintained through revision evidence.

Never silently substitute a normalized digest for an exact digest. Store normalization rules and generator versions beside every derived fingerprint. Normalization is a lossy interpretation and can collapse materially different code.

## 2. MinHash and locality-sensitive blocking

Andrei Broder's foundational paper, [*On the Resemblance and Containment of Documents*](https://doi.org/10.1109/SEQUEN.1997.666900), introduced min-wise signatures for estimating set resemblance. Charikar's [*Similarity Estimation Techniques from Rounding Algorithms*](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring04/cos598B/bib/CharikarEstim.pdf) formalizes locality-sensitive hashing and explains that min-wise collisions estimate Jaccard similarity. LSH is a candidate-generation technique: similar objects collide with higher probability, trading exactness for sublinear retrieval.

For sets (A) and (B), Jaccard similarity is

\[ J(A,B)=\frac{\|A\cap B\|}{\|A\cup B\|}. \]

With (k) independent MinHash coordinates,

\[ \widehat J(A,B)=\frac{1}{k}\sum\_{i=1}^{k}\mathbf{1}\[h_i(A)=h_i(B)\] \]

is an unbiased estimator under the standard assumptions, with variance (J(1-J)/k). At the worst case (J=0.5), 128 coordinates have a standard error of about 0.044. This is sufficient for blocking but not for treating a threshold estimate as a proof. Recompute exact Jaccard or a richer score on the returned candidates.

### Suitable code feature sets

Create separate signatures instead of mixing everything into one bag:

- Normalized token 3-, 5-, and 7-grams.
- Identifier-component shingles after camelCase/snake_case splitting.
- Alpha-normalized token shingles in which local variable names are replaced by scoped roles.
- AST production-rule shingles.
- Typed edge tokens such as `function --calls--> function`, including direction and port role.
- Data-flow and control-flow path shingles with bounded length.
- API signature features: parameter kind, normalized type, optionality, return type, exception/error channel, async/streaming mode.
- Dependency and import sets.
- Test-coverage, example-use, and runtime-trace edge sets.

Preserve the unnormalized and normalized lanes. Raw names help identify true copying and ecosystem conventions; alpha-normalized features help survive local renames. Combining them prematurely loses that diagnostic distinction.

### LSH banding

If a signature is divided into (b) bands of (r) rows, a pair with estimated similarity (s) becomes a candidate with probability

\[ P(\text{candidate}\mid s)=1-(1-s^r)^b. \]

This provides an explicit recall/candidate-volume control. Multiple lanes are preferable to one magic setting:

- A high-recall lane with fewer rows per band.
- A high-precision lane with more rows per band.
- Per-language or per-entity-kind parameters learned from labeled pairs.

Store the banding configuration and hash seed family in the index epoch. Changing them changes retrieval behavior and therefore invalidates reproducibility.

### Good uses

- Type-1/2 and many Type-3 code-clone candidates.
- Duplicate documentation, examples, tests, schemas, configuration blocks, and generated wrappers.
- Similar local neighborhoods expressed as sets of typed edge/path features.
- Corpus deduplication before expensive embedding.
- Detecting forked or vendored implementations even when formatting changed.

The primary [SourcererCC paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.06448) is an important code-specific precedent: an optimized inverted index and token-order filters scaled near-miss clone detection to a 250-million-line corpus. The broader lesson is that cheap feature blocking plus exact candidate comparison often beats applying an expensive semantic model to everything.

### Do not use MinHash for

- Sequence order by itself; set shingling only approximates order locally.
- Weighted feature frequencies unless a weighted method is used.
- Negative/signed weights.
- Type assignability or effect compatibility.
- Behavioral equivalence.
- Exact provenance or security-sensitive equality.

### Edge cases

- Define empty-feature behavior explicitly; an empty entity should not collide indiscriminately with every other empty entity.
- Exclude generated boilerplate or down-weight it in another lane, otherwise framework scaffolding dominates similarity.
- Salt or namespace features by schema version and feature family to prevent accidental cross-family comparison.
- Treat macros, conditional compilation, templating, notebooks, and generated code as separate occurrence contexts.

## 3. Weighted MinHash and consistent weighted sampling

Unweighted MinHash discards counts. That is often wrong for graphs: a component calling a database once is different from a component dominated by database calls, even if both edge-type sets are identical.

Sergey Ioffe's [*Improved Consistent Sampling, Weighted Minhash and L1 Sketching*](https://research.google/pubs/improved-consistent-sampling-weighted-minhash-and-l1-sketching/) gives a consistent weighted sampling construction whose collision probability corresponds to weighted Jaccard similarity and supports efficient retrieval/sketching for nonnegative weighted vectors.

For nonnegative vectors (x) and (y), generalized Jaccard is

\[ J_w(x,y)=\frac{\sum_i\min(x_i,y_i)}{\sum_i\max(x_i,y_i)}. \]

### Good weighted features

- Typed in-edge and out-edge frequencies.
- IDF-weighted token or identifier-component counts.
- Motif/graphlet histograms.
- Effect frequencies from runtime traces.
- Call-site frequencies or coverage-weighted edges.
- Evidence-weighted claims, provided weights remain nonnegative and provenance is retained.

### Do not use it for

- Signed preference vectors.
- Arbitrary learned embeddings.
- Claims where a rare but decisive edge must never be averaged away, such as `writes_secret`, `deletes_resource`, or `requires_gpu`.
- Compatibility decisions.

Put decisive constraints in exact fields and filters. Weighted MinHash should retrieve “similar overall profiles,” not excuse a disqualifying edge.

## 4. SimHash / random-hyperplane fingerprints

Charikar's [random-hyperplane construction](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring04/cos598B/bib/CharikarEstim.pdf) maps vectors to compact bit strings such that Hamming distance estimates angular distance. For two vectors separated by angle (\theta), one random hyperplane bit agrees with probability (1-\theta/\pi). Google's primary report, [*Detecting Near-Duplicates for Web Crawling*](https://research.google/pubs/detecting-near-duplicates-for-web-crawling/), demonstrates large-scale near-duplicate detection with SimHash-style fingerprints.

### Use SimHash for

- Extremely compact weighted token/edge/motif fingerprints.
- Approximate cosine/angular blocking when feature weights matter.
- Fast Hamming-radius lookup for likely duplicates.
- A second, independent near-duplicate lane whose errors differ from MinHash.

### Do not use SimHash for

- Estimating Jaccard similarity.
- Exact content identity.
- Semantic code search merely because both use cosine-like geometry; SimHash only preserves the supplied feature vector's angle.
- Deciding type, version, effect, or behavioral compatibility.

### Practical recommendation

Use at least 128 bits for the default corpus fingerprint and retain a 64-bit projection only if a measured memory/latency benefit justifies its higher variance. Query via chunked Hamming indexes or multiple substring tables, then compute full Hamming distance and exact feature similarity on candidates. Store the hyperplane seed/generator version.

At 100 million entities, a 128-bit raw fingerprint is only about 1.6 GB before index overhead. That makes SimHash attractive as a universal cheap lane, but its compactness must not be mistaken for accuracy across all meanings of similarity.

## 5. Graph hashing, typed neighborhood fingerprints, motifs, and paths

### 5.1 Weisfeiler-Lehman neighborhood refinement

The [Weisfeiler-Lehman graph-kernel paper](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v12/shervashidze11a.html) describes an efficient feature extraction scheme for labeled graphs; its runtime is linear in the number of edges times the number of refinement rounds. Each round relabels a node from its current label and the multiset of neighboring labels, producing subtree-like structural features.

For a typed, directed code graph, use a direction- and edge-aware variant:

\[ c_0(v)=H(\text{entity kind},\text{normalized type},\text{effect class},\text{local attributes}) \]

\[ c\_{t+1}(v)=H\left(c_t(v),\operatorname{sort}{H(\text{direction},\text{edge type},\text{port role},c_t(u)) : u\in N(v)}\right). \]

Materialize separate features for radii 0, 1, 2, and 3. Radius is semantic: one hop may describe the immediate API, while three hops may capture an architectural role but also introduce unrelated package context.

### Code-specific labels to preserve

- Entity kind and language-specific construct kind.
- Edge type and direction.
- Input/output port identity and cardinality.
- Normalized type plus native type handle.
- Async, stream, iterator, callback, resource, and ownership modes.
- Reads/writes/creates/deletes/network/process/secret effects.
- Static, dynamic, generated, inferred, or human-asserted evidence class.
- Applicability conditions such as platform, feature flag, version, and build profile.

### Use WL fingerprints for

- Finding functions, classes, modules, or package slices with similar local architecture.
- Rename-tolerant structural retrieval.
- Candidate generation for adapter or replacement discovery.
- Comparing API neighborhoods across languages after conservative type normalization.

### Do not use WL fingerprints as graph-isomorphism proof

WL refinement can map distinct graphs to the same features. The primary analysis in [*How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826) also shows that common neighborhood-aggregation GNNs cannot distinguish certain simple graph structures and characterizes their relationship to the WL test. A learned graph embedding therefore does not automatically fix this limitation.

When exact small-graph equivalence matters, use canonical labeling or an exact matcher after blocking. The official [nauty and Traces project](https://pallini.di.uniroma1.it/) provides canonical graph labeling and automorphism computation for supported graph classes. Even canonical graph isomorphism proves structural equality only under the chosen encoding; it does not prove program equivalence.

### 5.2 Graphlets and typed motifs

The [efficient graphlet-kernel paper](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v5/shervashidze09a.html) compares graphs using counts or samples of small subgraphs, typically three to five nodes, and provides sampling-based speedups when exhaustive enumeration is too expensive.

For code graphs, define a controlled typed-motif vocabulary rather than treating every source symbol as a label. Examples include:

- `handler -> validator -> service -> repository`.
- `producer -> queue -> consumer`.
- `source -> transform -> sink`.
- `function -> retry -> network call`.
- `parser -> AST -> visitor`.
- `resource acquire -> use -> release`.
- `read secret -> authenticate -> outbound request`.
- `test -> fixture -> target -> assertion`.

Use motifs to retrieve architectural roles and repeated patterns. Do not treat motif similarity as evidence that types line up or behavior matches. Rare high-risk motifs should also be emitted as exact flags, not only numeric counts.

### 5.3 Bounded typed paths and walk shingles

Graphs with the same local degree/motif counts may have different causal order. Add bounded paths such as:

- call paths of length 2–5;
- data-flow source-to-sink paths;
- effect paths;
- error propagation paths;
- test-to-assertion paths;
- import/dependency chains;
- runtime trace n-grams.

Index exact path tokens with BM25 and sketch their sets with MinHash. Bound length, collapse repeated cycles, and keep path provenance. Random walks are useful for recall but are stochastic and may overrepresent high-degree hubs; deterministic bounded path families are easier to explain and reproduce.

### 5.4 Hypergraphs and port-level structure

A call with multiple arguments, a tuple return, or a pipeline junction is naturally hypergraphic. Pairwise expansion can lose the fact that several ports participate in one invocation. Encode each invocation/hyperedge as a first-class node connected to ordered port nodes. Then WL, motif, and path fingerprints can preserve:

- argument position or name;
- co-membership in the same call;
- variadic groups;
- multiple outputs;
- error and effect channels;
- evidence tied to the invocation rather than only the callee.

Maintain two graph views:

1.  A precise port-level hypergraph for solving and verification.
2.  A projected entity graph for inexpensive discovery and visualization.

Record projection rules so fingerprints remain reproducible.

### 5.5 Identity-sensitive and identity-free graph hashes

Store both:

- **Occurrence-sensitive fingerprints**, including exact entity IDs, for change detection and provenance.
- **Role-normalized fingerprints**, replacing local IDs with scoped types/roles, for similarity across forks, revisions, and languages.

Do not blend them. A rename should preserve role similarity but change occurrence identity.

## 6. Code embeddings: what the evidence supports

### Primary precedents

- [CodeSearchNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.09436) formalized natural-language semantic code search and released roughly six million functions in six languages, but its challenge used only 99 natural-language queries and about 4,000 expert judgments. It is a foundational benchmark, not sufficient evidence for a universal existing-code retriever.
- [CodeBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08155) learns joint natural-language/programming-language representations and evaluates natural-language code search.
- [GraphCodeBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.08366) adds data-flow structure and structure-aware objectives, directly supporting the idea that code retrieval should not rely on token sequences alone.
- [UniXcoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.03850) combines code, AST, and comments and evaluates zero-shot code-to-code search.
- [CodeT5+](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07922) explores multiple architectures/objectives for code understanding and generation; it is relevant as an encoder candidate but not a reason to use a generative model for every query.
- [CoIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.02883) broadens evaluation to ten datasets, eight retrieval tasks, and seven domains, and reports that code retrieval remains difficult for contemporary systems.
- [CoQuIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11066) adds quality-aware retrieval across correctness, efficiency, security, and maintainability; its reported finding that leading retrievers often fail to distinguish buggy or insecure code from better alternatives is a decisive warning against treating semantic relevance as quality.
- [jina-embeddings-v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18902) is a contemporary example of task adapters plus single-vector and late-interaction multivector representations, including a code-search task. It is a candidate arm to benchmark, not an architecture dependency.

### What embeddings should do

- Translate vague user intent into a high-recall candidate set.
- Bridge natural-language descriptions and identifiers/code.
- Find cross-language or structurally different implementations with similar stated purpose.
- Retrieve examples and tests that express usage more clearly than declarations.
- Provide one feature family to a learned ranker.

### What embeddings should not do

- Establish exact identity or provenance.
- Decide whether types, serialization formats, runtimes, versions, or effects are compatible.
- Certify correctness, security, maintainability, license suitability, or package health.
- Select a reusable implementation without body/evidence resolution.
- Replace lexical search; exact identifier and rare technical-token matches are often decisive.

### Store facet vectors, not one “everything” vector

One vector that concatenates code, docstrings, package README text, examples, dependencies, effects, and graph context can become dominated by whichever facet is longest or easiest for the model. Prefer named representations:

- `purpose_vector`
- `input_contract_vector`
- `output_contract_vector`
- `effect_vector`
- `failure_vector`
- `example_vector`
- `implementation_vector`
- `graph_neighborhood_vector`
- `package_context_vector`
- `test_behavior_vector`

The query planner should choose relevant spaces and fuse their rankings. For example, “replace this parser without network access” should search purpose/implementation semantically but enforce `network=false` exactly.

### Version every representation

Every vector reference needs:

- model and checkpoint digest;
- tokenizer and library version;
- query/document instruction or prefix;
- truncation/chunking strategy;
- normalization and pooling;
- source facet and source content digest;
- dimension, quantization, and projection version;
- creation time and validity interval.

Never compare vectors from unrelated spaces as if their scores were calibrated.

### Late interaction

[ColBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832) keeps token-level representations and performs a cheap late interaction, preserving fine-grained matches while precomputing document representations. This is attractive when a single code/card vector blurs decisive tokens such as types, exceptions, or library names.

Use late interaction only after a cheaper lane reduces the corpus. Qdrant's official [hybrid and multi-stage query documentation](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/hybrid-queries/) demonstrates dense/sparse prefetch followed by a ColBERT-style multivector stage. The architecture pattern is valuable even if a different engine is selected.

## 7. Typed API compatibility is a solver problem, not a similarity problem

### Official precedents show that “compatible” has multiple meanings

- [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/) requires a declared public API and communicates the publisher's intent about incompatible and backward-compatible changes. A version number is metadata, not proof that the implementation honored the promise.
- Python's [typing protocol specification](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/protocol.html) defines structural assignability for protocol members.
- TypeScript's official [type compatibility documentation](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/type-compatibility.html) uses structural compatibility but explicitly documents deliberately unsound cases, including function-parameter behavior. Therefore, replaying the native compiler configuration matters.
- Rust's [SemVer compatibility guide](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/semver.html) distinguishes major, minor, and possibly-breaking changes and shows that types, traits, generics, layout, features, minimum compiler version, and platform requirements all affect compatibility.
- The current [OpenAPI 3.2.0 specification](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.2.0.html) is a programming-language-neutral HTTP interface description and integrates JSON Schema, but it covers a protocol surface, not arbitrary in-process language semantics.
- [JSON Schema 2020-12](https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core) provides a declarative vocabulary for JSON document structure and validation.
- The WebAssembly Component Model's [WIT reference](https://component-model.bytecodealliance.org/design/wit.html) models named interfaces, functions, types, async operations, streams/futures, imports, exports, worlds, packages, and versions. It is a strong design precedent for a cross-language port algebra, but it does not encode every language's ownership, reflection, macros, generics, ABI, or behavioral contract.
- Buf's official [breaking-change documentation](https://buf.build/docs/breaking/) separates generated-source compatibility from binary-wire and JSON-wire compatibility. A rename can break generated source while leaving wire format intact; one boolean `compatible` field is therefore inadequate.

### Recommended normalized type/port algebra

Preserve the native type and add a conservative normalized view:

``` text
Type :=
    scalar(kind, width, signedness, units?)
  | nominal(language, exact_symbol_id, type_arguments)
  | opaque(language, exact_symbol_id)
  | record(fields, openness, layout?)
  | variant(cases, openness, discriminant?)
  | tuple(items)
  | union(items)
  | intersection(items)
  | option(item)
  | result(ok, error)
  | list(item, bounds?)
  | set(item)
  | map(key, value)
  | callable(parameters, returns, errors, effects)
  | iterator(item) | stream(item) | future(item)
  | resource(handle_type, ownership, lifetime)
  | refinement(base, constraints)
  | unknown(reason)
```

Each port should also carry:

``` text
direction, name/position, cardinality, required/optional/default,
sync/async/stream/callback mode, mutability, ownership/borrowing,
encoding/media type/schema, error channel, effects,
preconditions, postconditions, platform/runtime/version constraints,
native compiler/type-checker profile, and evidence.
```

### Directional compatibility

For a candidate callable to substitute for a required callable:

- Candidate inputs must accept every input the requirement permits: required-domain values must be assignable to the candidate's domain.
- Candidate outputs must be assignable to the required outputs.
- Candidate preconditions must be no stronger.
- Candidate postconditions must be at least as strong for relied-upon claims.
- Candidate errors and effects must fit the caller's allowed sets or be handled by a verified adapter.
- Runtime, serialization, ownership, lifecycle, version, and platform constraints must intersect.

Represent the result as:

``` text
PROVED_COMPATIBLE | PROVED_INCOMPATIBLE | COMPATIBLE_WITH_ADAPTER | UNKNOWN
```

Every verdict should include rule IDs, source facts, compiler/schema checker versions, unresolved assumptions, and any required adapter path.

### Compatibility layers

Evaluate separately:

1.  **Shape/type assignability**
2.  **Source compatibility**
3.  **Binary/ABI compatibility**
4.  **Wire/serialization compatibility**
5.  **Runtime/platform compatibility**
6.  **Effect and policy compatibility**
7.  **Behavioral contract compatibility**

A candidate may pass one layer and fail another. Never collapse these layers before the route solver or receipt.

### Adapter discovery

Model adapters as verified primitives with typed ports and explicit loss/effect annotations:

- serialization/deserialization;
- sync/async bridges;
- iterator/stream/list conversions;
- unit conversions;
- schema version migrations;
- exception-to-result conversion;
- language/process/RPC boundaries;
- resource ownership wrappers.

Then solve composition as a constrained path problem. Adapter edges have costs for latency, allocations, information loss, risk, and proof status. Semantic similarity may propose adapters, but only the typed solver can admit them.

## 8. Hybrid retrieval and index architecture

### Why hybrid is the default

Elastic's official [hybrid-search documentation](https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/hybrid-search) combines full-text and vector retrieval and recommends RRF. pgvector's official [hybrid-search section](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#hybrid-search) similarly combines PostgreSQL full-text search with vectors and suggests RRF or a cross-encoder. These implementations reflect a sound general principle: lexical and semantic retrievers fail differently.

[RRF's primary paper](https://plg.uwaterloo.ca/~gvcormac/cormacksigir09-rrf.pdf) combines rankings with

\[ \operatorname{RRF}(d)=\sum\_{r\in R}\frac{1}{k+r(d)}. \]

Because it uses rank positions rather than incompatible raw score scales, RRF is an excellent deterministic baseline for combining BM25, graph, LSH, sparse, and dense lanes. It is not universally optimal; tune its window/constant and later compare calibrated or learned fusion against it.

### Recommended candidate lanes

1.  **Exact lane:** entity IDs, content hashes, package URLs, SWHIDs, release/version, native symbol IDs, fully qualified names, signatures, schema IDs.
2.  **Fielded lexical lane:** names, aliases, docstrings, signatures, type names, error names, effects, examples, dependencies, package summaries. Split identifiers but retain exact subfields.
3.  **Clone lane:** token/AST MinHash, weighted edge MinHash, SimHash, normalized-body hashes.
4.  **Graph lane:** WL labels by radius, motifs, typed paths, graph degree/role features.
5.  **Sparse semantic lane:** learned term expansion where its incremental recall justifies serving cost. [SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720) is the primary precedent for learned sparse representations that retain inverted-index retrieval.
6.  **Dense lane:** one or more measured code/card embeddings.
7.  **Late-interaction lane:** only on a bounded candidate pool.
8.  **Reranker lane:** deterministic feature model, local cross-encoder/SLM, or stronger model according to uncertainty and budget.

Run exact filters before expensive lanes when the engine can preserve ANN recall. If a vector engine applies filters after ANN candidate generation, it may return too few results. pgvector's [filtering and iterative-scan documentation](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#filtering) explicitly describes this failure and offers partial indexes, partitioning, and iterative scans. Measure filtered recall, not only unfiltered ANN recall.

### ANN choices and scale

- [HNSW](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320) offers a strong speed/recall tradeoff but has meaningful graph-memory and build/update costs.
- [FAISS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734) provides exact and approximate, compressed, CPU/GPU similarity-search building blocks and is appropriate for controlled offline experiments or specialized serving.
- [DiskANN](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/diskann-fast-accurate-billion-point-nearest-neighbor-search-on-a-single-node/) is a primary precedent for SSD-resident billion-point search when an all-RAM graph is uneconomic.
- pgvector documents both HNSW and IVFFlat: HNSW generally improves the query speed/recall tradeoff but builds more slowly and uses more memory; IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory but requires training/list/probe tuning.

Do not select an ANN structure by benchmark reputation alone. Benchmark on the actual vector distribution, filter selectivity, update rate, tenant partitioning, and target recall. For 100 million or more entities, compare at least:

- exact flat search on a sampled oracle corpus;
- HNSW;
- IVF-PQ or another compressed inverted-file configuration;
- SSD-oriented graph search such as DiskANN;
- binary or Matryoshka coarse retrieval followed by full-vector reranking.

### Multi-stage engine precedent

Qdrant's official [hybrid-query documentation](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/hybrid-queries/) supports dense/sparse prefetch, RRF, weighted fusion, formula scoring, nested stages, and multivector reranking. The valuable architectural idea is independent of vendor choice:

``` text
large cheap candidate pool
  -> smaller full-precision vector pool
  -> smaller late-interaction pool
  -> typed compatibility gate
  -> body/evidence resolution
```

### Score fusion

Start with RRF because it is deterministic and robust to uncalibrated score scales. Then evaluate:

- weighted RRF by query class;
- distribution-based score normalization;
- logistic or gradient-boosted ranking over lane scores, exact match flags, graph features, quality/evidence, and compatibility status;
- contextual bandits only after logging propensities and obtaining outcome labels.

Never learn only from clicks or LLM preferences. Optimize cost per independently verified success and preserve a quality/safety floor.

## 9. Proposed `EdgeFingerprintBundle`

The bundle is a versioned sidecar. Large signatures/vectors should live in immutable blob/index storage and be referenced by handle rather than copied into every entity card.

``` yaml
edge_fingerprint_bundle:
  schema: taedri.edge-fingerprint-bundle/v0
  entity_occurrence_id: "..."
  source_snapshot_id: "swh:1:..."
  native_symbol_id: "..."

  integrity:
    exact_content_sha256: "..."
    canonical_serialization_sha256: "..."
    canonicalization_profile: "python-ast-lossless/v3"

  lexical:
    raw_token_minhash:
      handle: "mh://..."
      coordinates: 128
      feature_profile: "token-5gram/raw/v2"
    alpha_token_minhash:
      handle: "mh://..."
      coordinates: 128
      feature_profile: "token-5gram/scoped-alpha/v4"
    weighted_identifier_simhash:
      bits: 128
      value: "..."
      feature_profile: "identifier-idf/v3"

  structure:
    ast_production_minhash:
      handle: "mh://..."
      feature_profile: "ast-production-3gram/v2"
    typed_edge_weighted_minhash:
      handle: "wmh://..."
      feature_profile: "typed-edge-frequency/v1"
    wl:
      radius_0: "..."
      radius_1: "..."
      radius_2: "..."
      radius_3: "..."
      profile: "directed-port-wl/v1"
    motif_vector:
      handle: "sparse://..."
      profile: "typed-graphlet-3-5/v1"
    path_minhash:
      handle: "mh://..."
      profile: "typed-path-2-5/v1"

  semantics:
    purpose_vector: "vec://model_epoch/..."
    contract_vector: "vec://model_epoch/..."
    implementation_vector: "vec://model_epoch/..."
    graph_context_vector: "vec://model_epoch/..."

  exact_constraints:
    normalized_input_types: ["..."]
    normalized_output_types: ["..."]
    effects: ["filesystem.read"]
    forbidden_effects: []
    runtimes: ["cpython>=3.11"]
    platforms: ["linux-x86_64"]

  provenance:
    extractor: "..."
    extractor_digest: "sha256:..."
    compiler_profile: "..."
    graph_schema_epoch: "..."
    index_epoch: "..."
    generated_at: "..."
```

### Important schema rules

- The bundle must be immutable for one exact occurrence and generator epoch.
- A missing fingerprint means `NOT_COMPUTED` or `NOT_APPLICABLE`, never an empty or zero fingerprint.
- Every approximate signature includes its feature profile, seed family, dimensionality, and normalization.
- Exact constraints are not blended into semantic vectors.
- Evidence edges retain generator, source span/trace, confidence, and applicability.

## 10. Recommended query waterfall

``` text
DemandIR + CodeSliceManifest
  |
  +-- exact identity/history/cache lookup
  |
  +-- hard eligibility filter
  |     language/runtime/platform/version/license/policy/effects
  |
  +-- deterministic lexical/structural query templates
  |     fielded BM25 + signature/type fields + exact edge predicates
  |
  +-- parallel candidate blockers
  |     MinHash | weighted MinHash | SimHash | WL | motifs | paths
  |
  +-- selective semantic recall
  |     sparse | dense purpose | dense contract | graph-context vector
  |
  +-- rank fusion
  |     RRF baseline, query-class weights only if evaluated
  |
  +-- exact candidate rerank
  |     exact Jaccard/Hamming/graph features + evidence/quality priors
  |
  +-- typed bidirectional route solve
  |     direct match or verified adapter path; tri-state uncertainty
  |
  +-- optional late interaction / local SLM rerank
  |
  +-- body resolution for finalists
  |
  +-- execution + independent verification
  |
  +-- exact receipt and learning signal
```

“Bidirectional” should mean exploring providers from requirements and consumers from produced types, not treating type compatibility itself as symmetric.

## 11. Storage implications at 100 million entities

Raw payload estimates, excluding database/index overhead, replication, alignment, metadata, and temporary build space:

| Representation                              | Raw bytes/entity | Raw size at 100M |
|---------------------------------------------|-----------------:|-----------------:|
| SHA-256                                     |               32 |           3.2 GB |
| SimHash 128-bit                             |               16 |           1.6 GB |
| Four 128-bit WL digests                     |               64 |           6.4 GB |
| 64 coordinates × 16 bits compressed MinHash |              128 |          12.8 GB |
| 128 coordinates × 32 bits MinHash           |              512 |          51.2 GB |
| 384-dimensional FP16 vector                 |              768 |          76.8 GB |
| 768-dimensional FP16 vector                 |            1,536 |         153.6 GB |

This argues for:

- Computing tiny exact/SimHash/WL features broadly.
- Computing multiple large MinHash and embedding facets selectively by entity value and query demand.
- Deduplicating before embedding.
- Using immutable shared signature blobs for identical bodies.
- Testing reduced dimensions, half precision, binary coarse search, and product quantization with full-precision reranking.
- Separating hot current releases from cold historical corpus tiers.
- Keeping index-generation recipes deterministic so cold tiers can be rebuilt.

Do not infer total deployment cost from raw vector size; HNSW links, posting lists, payloads, replicas, write amplification, and build headroom can dominate.

## 12. Evaluation plan

### Pair strata

Build a labeled corpus with at least these distinct pair types:

- Exact duplicates.
- Whitespace/comment-only changes.
- Local alpha renames.
- Literal changes that preserve or alter behavior.
- Reordered independent statements.
- Type-1, Type-2, Type-3, and behaviorally similar Type-4 clones.
- Same name, different behavior.
- Same purpose, different algorithm/language.
- Same graph neighborhood, incompatible types.
- Compatible types, incompatible effects or runtimes.
- Compatible only through a verified adapter.
- API evolution: source-compatible but wire-incompatible, and the reverse.
- Secure/correct implementation paired with semantically relevant insecure/buggy implementation.
- Generated boilerplate and framework templates as hard negatives.
- Version/fork/vendor lineage positives and unrelated lookalikes.

### Blocking metrics

For every fingerprint lane report:

- recall at fixed candidate budgets;
- candidates per query and p50/p95/p99;
- precision after exact reranking;
- index bytes/entity;
- build and incremental-update throughput;
- p50/p95/p99 query latency;
- per-language, per-entity-kind, and per-size performance;
- stability across package versions and index epochs.

### Retrieval and composition metrics

- Recall@1/10/100 and nDCG@10.
- MRR by query class.
- Type-compatible recall@k, not only relevance recall@k.
- Direct-route vs adapter-route success.
- Compile/type-check success.
- Sandbox test and property-check success.
- Independent verification success.
- Cost and tokens per verified success.
- False-safe and false-compatible rates.

### Required ablations

- Exact + BM25 baseline.
- Add raw-token MinHash.
- Add alpha-normalized MinHash.
- Add SimHash.
- Add each WL radius independently.
- Add typed motifs and paths.
- Add sparse retrieval.
- Add each dense facet independently.
- Add late interaction.
- Compare RRF, weighted RRF, calibrated linear fusion, and learned ranking.
- Compare similarity-only selection against typed-gated selection.
- Compare retrieved body injection against handle/card-first disclosure.

Tune thresholds separately by language and entity kind. A five-line serializer, a generated client, and a 500-line graph algorithm have different collision and semantic regimes.

## 13. Immediate build items

1.  Specify `FeatureProfile`, `FingerprintHandle`, `EdgeFingerprintBundle`, and `CompatibilityVerdict` schemas.
2.  Implement exact body and canonical-serialization SHA-256 with explicit normalization versions.
3.  Implement raw and alpha-normalized token shinglers for Python first; preserve source spans and scope maps.
4.  Implement AST-production and typed-edge/path feature emitters.
5.  Add 128-coordinate MinHash, weighted MinHash, and 128-bit SimHash with fixed, versioned seeds.
6.  Add directed typed WL radii 0–3, treating invocation/hyperedge and port nodes explicitly.
7.  Define a small typed motif vocabulary plus sampled graphlet counts.
8.  Build exact Jaccard, Hamming, and feature-level rerankers; never return only sketch estimates.
9.  Create fielded BM25 indexes with exact name/signature fields and identifier-split analyzed fields.
10. Benchmark at least CodeBERT/GraphCodeBERT/UniXcoder-class local encoders plus one current code-search embedding on the same frozen evaluation set.
11. Store separate purpose, contract, implementation, and graph-context vectors.
12. Implement deterministic RRF over named retrieval lanes and record each lane's rank contribution.
13. Define the normalized type algebra and native-language escape hatches.
14. Implement Python assignability by invoking a pinned native checker where possible; use normalized rules only as a conservative cross-language layer.
15. Add OpenAPI/JSON Schema, Protobuf/Buf, and WIT importers as separate contract profiles.
16. Model adapters as versioned graph entities with typed ports, effects, loss, cost, and evidence.
17. Return `UNKNOWN` rather than guessing when compatibility cannot be proved.
18. Build the clone/compatibility/quality pair strata before tuning thresholds.
19. Measure filtered ANN recall; test partitioning or iterative scans for selective constraints.
20. Emit a `RetrievalReceipt` containing index epochs, feature profiles, candidates, exact rerank values, compatibility rules, adapters, and final evidence.

## Primary and official source index

- Malkov and Yashunin, [*Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320).

- pgvector, [official project documentation](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector).
- Elastic, [Hybrid Search](https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/hybrid-search) and [RRF API](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/reciprocal-rank-fusion).
- Qdrant, [Hybrid and Multi-Stage Queries](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/hybrid-queries/).

## Bottom line

For existing-code processing, the strongest design is not “graph RAG plus embeddings.” It is a reproducible, typed, multi-index evidence system:

- exact hashes and IDs establish what object exists;
- MinHash, weighted MinHash, and SimHash cheaply block likely near-duplicates;
- WL, motifs, and paths describe structural roles at multiple radii;
- lexical, sparse, dense, and late-interaction retrieval bridge vocabulary and intent;
- a native-aware typed solver determines whether entities can compose;
- execution and independent verification establish whether the proposed reuse actually works.

That separation simultaneously improves recall, reduces token use, preserves deterministic tracing, and prevents a high semantic-similarity score from being mistaken for compatibility or correctness.

# Taedri CodeGraph: Implementation-Grade Repository Blueprint

> **ANNEX STATUS — TARGET REPOSITORY BLUEPRINT.** “Must support” and “first release”
> are requirements and milestones, not evidence that those jobs already pass.

## Recommended project and repository name

**Project:** Taedri CodeGraph
**Repository:** `taedri-codegraph`
**Python distribution:** `taedri-codegraph`
**Python import package:** `taedri_codegraph`
**CLI:** `tcg`
**MCP server:** `taedri-codegraph-mcp`

The name says exactly what the first product does: process existing code into an evidence-bearing, searchable graph. It does not tie the project to PyPI, Python, RAG, a specific database, or an LLM vendor. “Taedri Code Atlas” is a good UI/product name later, but `taedri-codegraph` is the least ambiguous engineering repository name.

## Product boundary

Taedri CodeGraph ingests an existing repository, package release, source archive, or build artifact and produces a versioned graph of code entities, occurrences, typed relationships, interfaces, effects, documentation, tests, provenance, and evidence. It then serves deterministic search, graph expansion, impact analysis, bounded code slices, version diffs, and compact agent-facing entity cards.

The initial vertical slice processes Python repositories and PyPI artifacts. Its contracts are language- and ecosystem-neutral from the first commit. Python is an analyzer plugin and a package-source adapter, not a special case embedded in the graph schema.

The first release must support these end-to-end jobs:

1.  Index a local Git working tree without importing or executing it.
2.  Index a pinned PyPI wheel or sdist by artifact digest.
3.  Resolve a package, module, class, function, method, field, variable, parameter, test, CLI command, or configuration item to an exact sidecar ID.
4.  Search by native name, qualified name, signature, docstring, behavior phrase, input/output shape, effect, package, file, or neighboring entity.
5.  Traverse definitions, references, calls, imports, exports, inheritance, overrides, reads/writes, types, tests, documentation, effects, and provenance in both directions.
6.  Generate a token-bounded `CodeEntityCard` or `CodeSliceManifest` with exact evidence pointers and explicit coverage gaps.
7.  Compare two releases or commits and distinguish exact changes from probabilistic lineage hypotheses.
8.  Expose the same capabilities through a CLI, a versioned API, and a compact MCP meta-tool surface.
9.  Re-run analysis deterministically, reuse unaffected facts, publish an atomic graph epoch, and reconstruct why every returned fact exists.
10. Allow deeper analysis and optional semantic enrichment without treating an LLM-generated statement as ground truth.

This is an existing-code intelligence layer. It is not initially an autonomous code editor, a source host, a package installer, a full IDE, or a replacement for SCIP, LSP, CodeQL, Tree-sitter, package URL, SWHID, SPDX, or SLSA. It bridges and preserves those systems.

## Non-negotiable design rules

### Preserve source names; assign sidecar identities

Do not globally rename variables, functions, or classes. Such rewrites break imports, public APIs, reflection, serialization, dependency injection, ORMs, foreign-function interfaces, stack traces, patches, and upstream upgrades. Attach collision-resistant IDs to exact source occurrences instead.

Use separate identity layers because they answer different questions:

- `PackageLineageID`: package family within an explicit registry authority.
- `ReleaseID`: exact ecosystem release coordinate.
- `SourceSnapshotID`: exact source revision/tree/content.
- `DistributionID`: exact wheel, sdist, archive, JAR, crate, image, or binary bytes.
- `BuildID`: exact recipe, toolchain, inputs, platform, and output.
- `FileContentID`: exact file bytes.
- `OccurrenceID`: exact byte range and role in an exact file.
- `RevisionEntityID`: exact entity within a source/build context.
- `ConceptID`: revisable lineage claim across revisions.
- `BehaviorID`: behavior observed under an explicit input, environment, and oracle.

An external entity ID should be derived from canonical CBOR and SHA-256, but the complete canonical identity key must also be stored and compared. The digest is an index key, not the only record of identity.

### Preserve native analyzer facts

Normalization must never destroy overload resolution, dynamic-dispatch alternatives, compiler flags, macro provenance, generated-source mappings, may/must semantics, path-sensitive flows, type-system details, or analyzer uncertainty. Every normalized assertion points back to the native payload digest, producer version, configuration digest, analysis run, and source/build scope.

### Treat every edge as an assertion with evidence

The graph does not contain timeless, omniscient edges. It contains scoped assertions:

- `asserted`: metadata, annotation, documentation, or manifest claim;
- `extracted`: parser, compiler, indexer, or package-reader result;
- `inferred`: static analysis, heuristic, statistical model, or LLM result;
- `observed`: runtime trace, example, or test result;
- `verified`: independently reproduced outcome or oracle result.

Absence does not mean false. Negative, unknown, ambiguous, and unsupported results require explicit representation.

### Acquire safely; execute only in a separate opt-in stage

Metadata, archives, and source must be inspectable without importing the package, running setup hooks, resolving dependencies, or evaluating arbitrary build code. Builds, examples, tests, and runtime probes are later opt-in analysis passes in a network-restricted sandbox with resource limits and exact receipts.

### Publish immutable epochs

Queries pin a `GraphEpochID`. Candidate fact shards are validated before an atomic manifest is published. An epoch records schema versions, source/artifact digests, analyzer versions/configurations, coverage, projection versions, and parent epoch. Updates create a new epoch; they never silently rewrite a pinned result.

### Use progressive analysis and progressive disclosure

Cheap deterministic passes cover the whole corpus. Precise, deep, dynamic, embedding, and LLM passes run only where their expected information value justifies cost. Agent responses begin with handles and compact cards; source bodies and large neighborhoods are resolved only after selection.

## Repository architecture

Use a modular monolith for the first release, with analyzers isolated behind a versioned subprocess/gRPC contract. This produces one installable local tool while allowing future analyzers and storage services to be implemented in any language.
